speechtext:

In reply to the secretary general's communication of June 29, he was informed in a communication of July 12 that the Canadian government were making available three destroyers for service with the unified command. To the secretary general's communication of July 14, the government replied on July 21, forwarding a copy of the Prime Minister's broadcast of July 19, in which he announced the willingness of the government to send a squadron of transport aircraft. Before calling the orders of the day I should like to make a brief statement. It has come to my attention, and I notice from yesterday's Hansard, a copy of which has just been handed to me, that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) raised the question yesterday afternoon that when I left the chair at that time for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on a certain resolution now before the committee a number of hon. members on both sides of the house did not hear me when I put the usual question, "Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?" The reason may have been that there was a certain amount of commotion in the house which did not wholly cease when I rose to put the question. This conduct is contrary to standing order 12(2), which reads as follows:
When Mr. Speaker is putting a question, no member shall walk out of or across the house, or make any noise or disturbance.
Had it been brought to my attention at that time that the question put was not fully heard, I would have put it a second time. In future I would ask all hon. members to remain quiet when any question is being put from the chair, and I would also ask any hon. member who does not hear what is being said from the chair to so indicate at the time. I am sure I shall have the full co-operation of all hon. members in this regard.

subtopic: CLOSING OF SALMON FISHING ON THE FRASER RIVER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: CLOSING OF SALMON FISHING ON THE FRASER RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) asked if I would make a statement with respect to sockeye salmon fishing on the Fraser river in British Columbia.
This season was the cycle year for the return of the run of sockeye salmon spawned in 1946. One of the races in this cycle year, known as the Adams river run, was expected to return to the Fraser river system in large volume following excellent escapement to the spawning grounds in 1946. Unfortunately the run has not materialized in the volume expected, and in fact is estimated to be less than 20 per cent of either of the cycle years 1942 or 1946.
The international Pacific salmon fisheries commission is the joint agency responsible, under the treaty between Canada and the United States, for the preservation and rehabilitation of the Fraser river sockeye runs. The commission has been watching the situation most closely to see that there is escapement to the spawning grounds to ensure a return of this race of fish in 1954. The international salmon commission took action to assure sufficient escapement and to provide opportunity for Canadian fishermen to catch their share of the available sockeye salmon on a parity with United States fishermen by closing the waters of Puget sound to fishing by the United States fleet. This closure became effective at nine p.m. on August 30, until September 6, when the sockeye will have passed through American waters.
Because of the disappointing volume of this particular run of fish-the Adams river run- and in the interests of conservation, information reached the department on Tuesday afternoon that the commission has announced that effective at eight a.m. on Thursday, September 7, until October 2, the Fraser river, including
320	HOUSE OF
Defence Appropriation Act the gulf of Georgia, will be closed to fishing, except that during this period nets with a mesh size of eight inches or greater may be used.
Canadian fishing operations can still continue in the straits of Juan de Fuca and in that portion of the gulf of Georgia known as area 18-Pender island. It is not likely any sockeye will be caught in the areas remaining open to fishing, since the Adams river run has passed through these waters. Fishing here will be conducted for species other than sockeye.
It is not possible to reach any conclusions concerning the causes of the serious failure of the 1950 Adams river sockeye run until an analysis can be made of the catch and escapement statistics. It is reported to the department that escapement to the spawning grounds of the earlier runs of sockeye to the Fraser river system this season has been good, and reports indicate the grounds are adequately seeded.
Up until August 30 the United States fishermen had caught 1,191,000 sockeye from the runs to the Fraser river system. The Canadian catch up to September 4 was 736,000 fish. It is hoped this difference of 455,000 fish will to some extent be reduced when Canadian sockeye fishing operations are resumed on October 2.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, September 5, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for national defence and security-Mr. Abbott-Mr. Dion in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose last evening I had mentioned that there were some questions that I wished to direct to the Minister of National Defence with regard to the money to be provided for future commitments in connection with the defence forces and which might be incurred during the present year.
According to the resolution these commitments for the navy, army and air force amount to $409,257,821, with $5,310,000 for research-a sum of huge proportions. This idea of asking for money for which detailed estimates are not presented to parliament is something which has been introduced only in recent years. Normally it is the custom to present detailed estimates of the money to be expended. During the last session of parliament $144 million was asked for in the way of future commitments, and in the year previous to that $145 million odd was asked
[Mr. Mayhew.l

for. We have had no accounting to date as to how that $290 million, in round figures, has been expended. We have had no information as to whether any portion of that amount has been spent, whether it is all gone or whether it is still available. I submit that the Minister of National Defence should explain to the house how he has spent that $290 million which was given to him in the form of a blank cheque before he comes back and asks the house for another blank cheque for over $400 million. I hope the minister will not only be able to give us an account of what has been spent up to date of the blank cheques which he has received already, but will also indicate, so far as he can, how he intends to spend this vast amount of over $400 million for which he is now asking.
The people of this country are concerned about the tremendous expenditures which have been made on national defence. They have been disturbed by the events of recent months which seem to indicate that even with the expenditure of this money we have not a force which is capable of answering the call made upon this country, even though that call may not have been foreseen. There are doubts as to whether the force which we now have is even competent of carrying out the task that has been assigned to it.
During this session I have questioned whether the airborne brigade has reached the standard of efficiency which the people of this country believed it had, based upon the statements made in the house by the Minister of National Defence and supporters of the government. I picked up a paper today which contains a statement by Brigadier Rockingham, made only yesterday, with regard to the efficiency of this airborne brigade. Remember that the airborne brigade is the only force we have in Canada that is considered capable of being able to act immediately in the event of acts of aggression against Canada. I am not talking about acts of aggression outside of Canada. We were told it could not be sent out of Canada because it was the only force in Canada which was ready to resist an act of aggression, even a diversionary raid. Dealing with the Royal 22nd regiment, the regiment from the province of Quebec now in the active army, Brigadier Rockingham, the commander of the special Korean force, is reported in today's Montreal Gazette to have said in Quebec city yesterday:
The first battalion-	.
That is the regular battalion.
-of the 22nd has been concentrated as a battalion for the first time in some years at Valcartier.

This is a battalion of the airborne brigade force which is expected to be able to engage the enemy immediately. It is now being concentrated, for the first time in a number of years, for battalion training at Valcartier. Then Brigadier Rockingham goes on to say, referring to troops of that battalion:
Troops at Rivers, Man., undergoing parachute training, and the detachment at St. Johns, Que., have been recalled. Reason for the move is that the parent unit-
The Royal 22nd regiment of the active force.
-will be responsible for the training of the reinforcement stream for the special force battalion.
I made the statement yesterday, repeating what I had said last week, that the airborne brigade is not ready to act immediately as a formation in the defence of Canada. I said that their men might be poured into battle piecemeal, but they could not fight as a coherent organized unit because they had never been trained together and were unable to work as a team, inasmuch as they had had no formation training. I pointed out that certain elements of the brigade were still lacking. The statement made by Brigadier Rockingham confirms my statements, and in fact hasi emphasized them by pointing out that one of the battalions has not even received unit training, let alone working as a unit within a brigade.
It is therefore quite obvious that before the airborne brigade could fight as a brigade it would require a further period of training. I now ask the Minister of National Defence if he will tell us how long it will take, in his opinion and in the opinion of his military advisers, before the airborne brigade will be in a position to fight as a brigade, and not merely piecemeal as separate units. I would ask him also what steps are being taken to accelerate that further training. The remarks made by Brigadier Rockingham only underline the remarks I made last night, in which I pointed out the extreme difficulty that exists when you give a dual role to one body of troops, the dual role being to be ready to protect our northern frontier, and at the same time to provide for the expansion of our reserve army forces.
It is obvious that the training of the Royal 22nd regiment to carry out what is considered to be their primary role, that of acting in co-operation with other units of the airborne brigade, has been disrupted in order that they may be withdrawn to carry out the secondary role of providing for the expansion of the second battalion of the Royal 22nd regiment, their share of the special service force now being organized for Korea.
Defence Appropriation Act
I asked a number of questions during the debate last night. To summarize them briefly, so far as the navy is concerned, the people of Canada want to know when the nine or ten new ships now under construction will be available. They want to know when the new anti-submarine vessels will be available for the defence of Canada to replace the ships of the Royal Canadian Navy which have now gone to Far Eastern waters. They want to know when the reconditioning of ten destroyers will be completed, and when trained men will be made available to man these vessels.
So far as the army is concerned, the question I ask is when will the airborne brigade be ready as a brigade, as a formation and not as small detachments, to be able to fight in the defence of Canada if need be. I have asked when the personnel of the reserve army will be ready to provide not only expanded forces for the defence of this country, but also the overseas forces which may be required if we are asked in the near future to carry out any operations in accordance with the wishes of the United Nations or our agreements under the North Atlantic treaty. What steps are being taken to bring the reserve forces up to a standard of readiness which will enable them to be placed in the field in a reasonably short time, either before or after an emergency has actually developed? The minister said that he had it all taped down to the last man as to how many men would be required for the navy, army and air force. The people of Canada want to be reassured and told that they will be ready and available within a reasonably short time, or they want to be told that the plans which have been in effect up to the present are not providing such training and such means of equipping and mobilizing the force as will enable reserve formations to be ready shortly. If that should be the case, then they want to know what steps are being taken by this government to correct those deficiencies. It is no use making the statement that a recruiting drive is to be undertaken for the reserve army. It is true that there are some excellent units in the reserve, but the training of a great many units is deficient, and many are short in manpower. They do not have enough men today to bring their strength up to a quarter of their effective establishment. I know the difficulties in connection with recruiting forces. Let the minister tell us what steps are being taken, and the exact position of the reserve army.
With respect to the air force, we have been told that we are getting certain new planes- the CF-100, the F-86, the Mustangs, and air-
322

Defence Appropriation Act craft for our carrier Magnificent. We want to know when those will be ready and available. We want to know when those aircraft will be actually provided to the various squadrons of the R.C.A.F., or placed on the Magnificent. We want to know when it is estimated there will be a sufficient number of trained pilots to operate these various aircraft.
I have tried to summarize some of the questions to which I think hon. members must have the answers before they can carry out the instructions given by the Prime Minister, examine and decide for themselves whether the steps being taken by this government are sufficiently speedy and adequate. I know there will be people in this country and members of this house who will say that if this information is given to the house, published in the press and made available to the people of Canada, the result will be to break security and to give information which may be of value to an enemy, should that enemy not have the information in his possession already. We have suggested two possible solutions. My leader has asked time and again for a committee, in which such information could be given. The government has turned down that suggestion. Then my leader made the only other practical suggestion I can think of which would enable hon. members to obtain the information it is their bounden duty to obtain-that is, that we have a secret sitting of this house, from which the public would be excluded, in which the Minister of National Defence could answer all questions without fear of any leak in the essential security arrangements of the country.

speechtext:
I will deal as quickly as possible with some of the points raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo. It would partly meet his request, and also have the information at one place in Hansard, if I gave in the briefest possible manner a summary of the actual work being done to accelerate the development of our armed forces. This information has been given before. Perhaps I should have given it again yesterday during the course of my statement, but I thought it was not necessary. In view of the remarks of my hon. friend, however, I believe I should do so at this time. Dealing briefly with the three services I shall give such information as can be made available, and then deal with some of the other points.
Dealing first with the Royal Canadian Navy:
1. Manpower. The ceiling of 9,600 officers and men has been increased by 40 per cent to a total of 13,440 all ranks. Recruiting to this total will be carried on at the rate of 240 or more per month, which is a planned figure based upon increased training facilities.

2.	When the program for the commissioning of ships has been completed, the total of 13,440
will be divided half and half between those at sea and those on shore, which is considered everywhere to be a desirable division.
3.	Ships. We already have under construction one icebreaker, three anti-submarine vessels, four minesweepers and a gate vessel. We will add to those a number of additional anti-submarine vessels, minesweepers and gate vessels. The number has been recommended by the Department of National Defence to the maritime commission and the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which are now examining the possibilities of placing orders and getting this work under way immediately. It is not possible to give the planned rate of production. That information must be based first on the development of plans of new vessels, and second on the speed with which yards can tool up and get going on complicated types. That is being pressed on, but obviously the vessels will only begin to come into production in 1951, and successively from then on as they are built.

1.	Manpower. The establishment has been increased from 18,278 by forty per cent to a total of 24,950. We plan on the intake for aircrew of 150 every six weeks, and we also hope to get 450 groundcrew per month. The figures under the old program were 100 groundcrew and 40 aircrew per month.

3.	Maritime operations. Squadrons of Lancasters are being or have been converted to maritime operations and will be built up to full fighting strength. The long-range transportation squadron is being increased from eight to twelve North Stars. The squadrons for

4.	Training. Facilities are being increased to provide for the training of more than three times as many aircrew for Canada, but this is in addition to the one hundred for the North Atlantic treaty nations and two hundred for the United Kingdom.
5.	Equipment. Construction of F-86 planes by Canadair Limited at a greatly accelerated rate, and of the CF-100 as well as Orenda engines. In addition we have purchased and will be taking delivery of the 100 Mustangs as an interim measure.
These facts and figures have been before-hon. members, but 1 thought it desirable that they should be put before them again. Against this background may I take up one or two-of the points raised by some hon. members opposite, and go just as far as I can in. dealing with them.
The hon. member for Broadview made a suggestion, put forward reasonably and seriously, for a new type of formation in Canada. As I understood his plan, it was that we-recruit either an armoured division or an; infantry division plus an armoured brigade: All the recruits would serve full time long enough to make them fully trained soldiers. They would then be returned to their positions in civil life. On their return to civil life they would form a special reserve in the army, the officers of which would be paid a retaining fee of $30 per month and other ranks $20 per month. In the time at his disposal the hon. member was not able fully to develop his plans for this force.
The first thing to consider is whether or not such a force would be desirable, even if it could be achieved, and what it would accomplish. In that connection hon. members know that the strength of an infantry division under our system is at present about 20,000 officers and men. It is estimated that to train a formation of that kind, or any other considerable body of troops, requires one trainer to look after training and administration for each trainee. That proportion was usual during the war, and it is usual in our own and other services. Sometimes we here can reduce the number, but ordinarily that is about what it works out to be. To provide a training establishment, therefore, for these 20,000 would! require about 10,000 more men, which would! mean we would have some 30,000 personnel; involved in the actual work of training and' administration of these troops as well or in; the division itself. One difficulty we see in the plan is this: what do you do for officers, N.C.O.'s and tradesmen, the training of whom ordinarily takes more than a year? It does not in wartime, it is true. Are these men to form part of the division and be trained with it and then returned to civil life? Then we come to the question: what would the division be for? With that, I come to the consideration of what kind of defence forces we need in Canada for the defence of Canada. This has been dealt with a great number of times, but again I would be glad to go over it briefly.
The hon. member for Broadview spoke as if he envisaged large scale amphibious landings on the northwest coast of North America. Everything can be envisaged, and everything is possible in modern war at some date or another. In the immediate future I can assure him and assure the house, without a breach of security, that that is not envisaged at all. References to plans that have appeared in United States publications and an examination of the kind of defences that the United States themselves think desirable in Alaska would indicate that they have the same appreciation; Obviously they do not think an invasion on that scale likely. Certainly we do not. It is difficult enough to launch a considerable amphibious operation across the narrow waters of the bay of Biscay and the English channel, with a build-up over a couple of years even though it was supported by overwhelming air power. But to envisage such an operation being carried out by the only possible aggressor with such surface and other vessels as we know him to have, is, we think, at the present time extremely unlikely.
The scale of attack that might be made on this continent must of course change with time, and it is changing. Where the risk of even a diversionary raid or a diversionary attack was slight indeed three years ago, it is an actual possibility today; but the scale still is not expected to be anything other than that required to lead us to keep on the North American continent more forces than we should otherwise keep here. In other words, it is not envisaged as a possibility at the present time that the only possible aggressor should carry out an operation of attack and landing, either across the water or by

air, on a scale sufficient to hold any considerable portion of this continent for any considerable length of time.
I should make it perfectly clear, as I have done again and again, that, given the conditions of modern warfare, there is no way on earth in which a country of three and a half million square miles can be made impregnable against attack. It could not be done, with all the resources of the United Kingdom, during the second world war. In spite of a radar screen, interceptors and gallant aircrew, still a considerable proportion of German aircraft got across; and the reverse was true also. It is therefore quite impossible, quite unthinkable, and it would be militarily wrong, for us to plan to have the kind of defences that would prevent any and every attack by air. That is not possible. 1 have indicated that a dozen times.
But what we can do is to make it just as difficult as we can, and that means having radar protection extending over the approaches-radar stations backed up by interceptor squadrons. Those are being developed. One of the things that an enemy wants to know more than anything else is the location of radar stations. As hon. members know, radar at the present time operates only to the physical horizon. You therefore cannot have a radar screen, or grid really, over the whole North American continent. We have to spot these stations at important and vulnerable points. Then it becomes extremely important that their exact location should not be given officially, and we have never announced their locations. Some announcements have appeared in the press, and I have indicated why it is desirable that these announcements should not be made in the press giving their exact locations.
Everyone knows that some kind of construction is going on in some localities; that fact cannot be kept secret. But that is quite a different thing from giving officially the exact location; because giving a thing in that way not only gives the information to the only possible enemy, but enables him- and this is extremely important-to check the efficiency of his own intelligence and to verify which of his possible sources are accurate and which are not. We are therefore not giving the locations of such sites, but they are being pressed forward.
While the great area of North America makes it difficult to prevent a raid, on the other hand it gives us great possibilities of defence in depth; and we can see the advantage of that from what the twenty miles of the English channel meant during the darkest days of the war. Here at all points, except over the Bering strait, there are


hundreds of miles, or even thousands of miles of distance; so that if enemy aircraft are detected, the chances of their being brought down are considerable-much greater than in the shorter distances in Europe-provided that there is a system of detection and interception. That system is being worked on and pressed forward. But as I indicated last year, let nobody think that we have more than a beginning of this type of defence.

Perhaps I might go on and deal with another point arising out of the suggestion of the hon. member for Broadview. The division suggested by the hon. member would consist of some 20,000 men, who, at the end of their training period, which certainly would be more than seven months, would return to civilian life. They no longer would remain a division in being. They would be a division nearly in being, and how nearly in being they would be would depend upon how long it was since they had trained as a division. We have in the special force a rather large brigade group, and then in addition we will have in the special force a group of reinforcements of almost sixty per cent. I think anything would be advisable which would strengthen our forces and our defences against the enemy. But what is advisable must also be possible and desirable, having regard to other possible uses of our resources, our men and our money.
I suggest that at the present time it would be much better for us to get on with the job of developing an air force in being, arming it, equipping it and training it, than to have a

division in being located in Canada and staying there. Also it must be obvious to hon. members that a division of the type envisaged by the hon. member for Broadview, an armoured division of the kind he mentioned, would involve a tremendous amount of equipment. It has been stated in the United States that to equip an armoured division of the type they have, which is generally similar to the type we have, equipped with the latest weapons, would cost over $500 million. I am informed that to equip an infantry division would cost $100 million. As I indicated to the committee yesterday, we have considerable quantities of equipment available. The question is under discussion whether that equipment could not better be used for the defence of Canada as well as for the defence of the north Atlantic free nations and freedom everywhere, if it were in the hands of countries in Europe rather than in our mobilization stores. That would mean that we would be without equipment pending its replacement by equipment still to be made in Canada or purchased from other countries.
The hon. member for Nanaimo referred, in very suitable terms, I think, to the quality of the men in the brigade groups. He said that they have never trained together as a formation. That is perfectly correct. I must say at the present time it is not considered that it would operate in Canada as a brigade group, as a single functioning formation. That will become desirable in the future, and consequently that training will be proceeded with.
Of course it has a headquarters staff. Some members have suggested that it only had the one battalion that was in good shape, but I suggest that they tell that to the Royal Canadian regiment and the 22nd! While the Princess Pats were the first to be trained as paratroopers, the other regiments are progressively being put through training and they are doing well.

The numbers taking training have increased materially, just as have the numbers of men in the reserve forces, as I indicated yesterday. Hon. members have suggested that the number should be larger. No one would be more pleased to see it larger than I. We have made every effort to make it larger, and the result is that the number has almost trebled in the last three years. But we want it still larger. Everything that we know of is being done to secure the attendance of men at the camps. They like the camps, but they find it difficult to leave their families to take their holidays at camp. We want to maintain the rate of recruiting for all three services, and that will require the co-operation of all people. I ask particularly for the co-operation of all hon. members. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the procedure we are following is most unfortunate; the result is that most of this morning has been practically wasted. We have before us two sets of estimates that tell us nothing, or at least nothing that can be discussed specifically. The first one is the cash program, which totals some $142,200,200. I assume that that represents the immediate requirements, what the minister wants right away. The next deals with future years' program, totalling $414,567,821. I assume that this is necessary in order to plan for war in the future.
The discussion this morning clearly indicates the necessity of setting -up a defence committee. I do not think the discussion we have carried on this morning has provided much information, and it has definitely tended to create confusion in the country. You cannot sit down in this House of Commons and discuss these estimates and plan the defence of the country with the minister across the floor except on a partisan basis. Whether or not you like it, that is exactly how it will be discussed here. The minister feels that anything said by members on this side is criticism of government policy. On the other hand the opposition feel that it is their duty to pick as many holes as they possibly can.
A year ago, and at the present session, it was suggested from this side of the house that a defence committee should be set up. I think the matters we are trying to discuss now, such as army personnel, requirements, and so on, should be left to a defence committee, because the discussion can go on here forever and you will never arrive at a conclusion. At the last session a defence bill was introduced that would have occupied much of the time of the house if it had not been sent first to a committee. It went to a defence committee and the committee did an excellent job. They boiled down the discussion and arrived at conclusions. The important thing was that men from the army, navy and air force, who knew what they were talking about, were called before the committee. The present situation is not fair to the minister, and he is not fair to himself. It does not do any 

good to come into the house and carry on the kind of discussion that has been taking place this morning. I am more confused now than I was when the house opened as to whether we have a navy, army, or air force at all.
There are a lot of questions that I should like to ask, but I do not want to ask the minister on the floor of the house because I do not think it would be fair. I should like to ask people from the navy, army and air force whose responsibility it is to do certain things with respect to defence and offence. I suggest that we should set up such a committee.
The second point I have in mind is that all the money we are appropriating under these estimates is going to be spent by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. While we are voting money for the navy, army and air force, since the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been designated as the defence purchasing authority it is going to be spent by his department. Most of the questions we should be asking should be directed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I want to say a few words on that aspect of the situation. Providing the money is an easy thing, because the money is there; but we are not going to fight a war in Korea or anywhere else just by passing estimates. Something has to be done with the money.
For a minute or two I think we should take inventory of our own actions since 1945. I have always felt we were rather foolish in dismantling the equipment we had when the last war was supposed to be terminated. That war has never terminated. The shooting has never stopped. It is just a matter of changing enemies. The war has still been going on. In the face of that situation we were in a great hurry to scrap our merchant marine, tear up our air force, let barracks go by the board and get rid of what we called surplus war materials. We threw away hundreds of millions of dollars worth of war equipment that we could very well be using now, and the price we received represented only about ten per cent of the value of the equipment when we threw it away. It is gone. Everybody was in such a hurry to get back to what was called a free economy. We did so, and now we are starting in where we started in 1939 to try to put the nation on a war footing.
Why do we not merely pass an order in council handing over the future defence of the institutions of this country to the system of free enterprise and those who are running it? Let them fight the next war, plan it themselves, and see where we wind up. With all the talk against planning and socialism, it

is now being demonstrated that we must plan, and, whether or not governments like it, they are going to have to interfere more and more in the economic processes of the country. That is the kind of world that is developing. We are starting all over again now. We are going to take the economy of Canada and establish certain controls in order to put it on a war footing.
I suggest that first of all we should take the discussion of the mechanics of the navy, army and air force, and the planning for defence or offence, off the floor of the House of Commons and out of the realm of politics. We should set up a committee where we can call the heads of the different departments and talk over these matters with the men who are specifically charged with responsibility. If we do that I think we will get away from politics.
Then there is a suggestion I have for the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he begins to provide new buildings, ships, and so forth. We scrapped our merchant marine right after the last war. They did a good job. They were the supply line from this continent to the battlefields of the world. As soon as the war was over we got rid of the merchant marine. The merchant navy did not receive very good treatment, but we are going to need them again. They are going to be just as important in the next conflict as they were in the last. We are starting to build ships. We should not have given away the ones we had at the conclusion of the last war. We should have at least put them in mothballs for a few years.
With the lessons of the past so fresh in the memories of those whom we may want to sail our ships, one of the first things that should be done is to tell prospective merchant service personnel that we are going to treat them in the same way as the armed forces. We should tell them that we are going to bring them under the veterans charter, and that they are to have all the rights and privileges that veterans of the last war enjoy. That is one of the first things that should be done, because the merchant marine is a most important arm of our services.
In planning the production of the country I think we made the mistake in the last war -and I am saying this for the benefit of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-of overdeveloping plant and equipment in the central provinces. Such a procedure does not strike a good balance in the economy in peacetime, and it is definitely not good policy to have too great a centralization of war plants at any one point where they can be knocked out very easily. As we are going to build our war 69262-22
Defence Appropriation Act machine all over again, I think this time we should consider decentralization. I should like to remind the minister about the plate mill at Sydney, Nova Scotia, which was dismantled on the termination of the last war. It did an excellent job in providing plate for shipbuilding purposes, ninety per cent of which we import from the United States. The guts are gone from the plate mill. During my lifetime we have equipped it twice. During the last war it was equipped with modern up-to-date machinery, six hundred men were employed, and it did a good job. My information is that it was sold to the government of Czechoslovakia and is now behind the iron curtain. The frame of the building is there, however, and the government might consider re-equipping it.
Then I wanted to say something that should interest both trade and commerce and transport. During the last war we discussed in this house time and again the bottleneck at the strait of Canso; the hon. member for Cumberland raised that question again this morning. We were told that as soon as the war was over something would be done about it. We definitely remember the difficulties we had getting coal up the St. Lawrence, because of that bottleneck. We also remember that we spent enough money building auxiliary services for Point du Chene to complete that project, because submarines were in the St. Lawrence. Personally I believe that should be considered a war project. One-third of Canada's basic steel is produced on the island of Cape Breton, and a large percentage of our coal is there as well. Those two commodities are essential at all times, and particularly in wartime; therefore I believe we should take immediate steps to improve transportation facilities there so that we can make use of those materials, and get at them in a hurry.
This morning the minister tabled correspondence between the province of Nova Scotia and the federal government with regard to the trans-Canada highway. We have not seen it; I do not know what it is, but in any case the agreement has been too long delayed. The trans-Canada highway was part of that Canso project which was held up by the provincial government, in fact, because they wanted it to conform to the width of the trans-Canada highway. If agreement has now been reached, in view of the importance of that project if and when we get into difficulties I believe steps should be taken immediately to complete the bridge project. People say: Oh, it will take three years, or five years-but you know we are the greatest procrastinators in the world. I remember that in 1942, during the last war,

Defence Appropriation Act I was arguing for this very thing. I was told then that it would take five years, that it would cost $56 million, and all that sort of thing. I picked up a survey of that project made in 1906 by the Waddell-Hardesty Company of New York. At the time I was discussing it, during the war, that company sent an eminent engineer, Mr. W. J. Kemp, who spent a few days with me revising the plans and bringing the estimate of cost up to date. He told me at that time that if their company were given a contract to bridge the strait of Canso they could do it in six months. Further they said they could get priority on steel in the United States because the Americans were in Newfoundland at the time, and they wanted those facilities improved. Now, with Newfoundland linked up with us and with the stimulation of trade between the mainland and that island, there is a definite need for the best possible transportation facilities in that part of the country to move the large amount of steel and coal that is necessary to the general economy of the country. This project should be considered as part of the construction necessary for war.

speechtext: Before the hon. member leaves that point, may I ask what Mr. Kemp estimated would be the cost of the Canso project?

His estimate of cost at that time was around $20 million. The final figure arrived at by the government was $13,500,000, so he was not far out in his rough estimate.
I should like to say to the Minister of National Defence that the organization and treatment of the reserve army leaves much to be desired, as has always been the case. I have always looked upon the reserve army as the base for the army of the future if and when it should become necessary to have one. In the part of the country I come from, where I think the percentage of enlistments in the last two wars compares favourably with that in any other part of Canada, the reserve army does not even have a place to drill. You appoint a few officers; they pick up some personnel, and then they are left to themselves. In Sydney, Glace Bay and various other towns I have been spoken to many times by reserve army officers who want to know if they could not get a building to which they could take the boys on drill nights and at least have some cover and some room to manoeuvre while they were taking instruction. There is nothing at all.
Considering the position in which the average man is placed in the reserve army, I often wonder how you get any men at all. You take in a man and make him a captain. He is paid $280 a year, I think, and has to buy his own uniform. Then you put him in

charge of equipment worth $50,000 or $60,000, and make him responsible for it. He must pay income tax on his $280, which often puts him in a higher tax bracket. As I say, I often wonder why a man gets into the reserve army at all on that basis, because it will cost him at least $1,000 a year, and in addition he has to accept responsibility and give up his leisure time. I believe someone should take a good look at the arrangements now in effect and revise them very considerably. If the reserve army had been properly handled, properly set up and properly looked after, you could have raised your Korean force from the reserve army overnight, trained and ready to go. I suggest to the minister that these arrangements should be overhauled immediately.
My main plea, however, is to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that in spending all this money, erecting these plants, buying equipment, and doing all the things he did in the last war, he will see to it that this is not all centralized in one area where it might be knocked out overnight by one plane if it happened to get through. I do not look at this situation any longer in terms of what is going on in Korea; I think we are too late for that. It does not look so good; for out of Korea something else is likely to come. I believe the planning we do now should not be of a temporary nature, and I do not think we should be too complacent about it. It should be permanent; it should be the best, and it should not be measured in terms of money.
I would point out to the Minister of National Defence something else that is not helping recruiting. Already I have had letters from the parents of boys who have gone into the service, telling me that the barrack conditions under which they are starting to serve are terrible. The food is bad; there is not enough of it; the barracks are dirty and a complete mess. When a kid will write home and tell his parents that sort of thing it must be pretty bad. I suggest that the minister take a look at the conditions under which this force is living, at least in district No. 6, since that is where my complaints came from. It is the little things, mind you, that stick. Generally I find that if you look after the little things the big things will look after themselves.
We had an incident at Petawawa a few days ago which will not help voluntary recruiting, either. What must have been the reaction of a father or mother with a young son who may be going into the service, on picking up a newspaper and reading that five or six boys were injured or lost their

lives in training at that camp? My first reaction was that the instructors were too young; two kids, twenty-one years of age, given raw recruits. But I think another instance of sheer neglect was the training with live ammunition, particularly heavy mortar bombs with detonators, placed in the hands of kids who knew nothing about them. I believe somebody should be rapped over the knuckles for neglect. Such things do not help recruiting, because parents are reluctant to send their boys when they read of things like that. Old seasoned veterans should be the instructors, men whose stability and mentality has been tested for the job, and not children such as were involved in that particular incident.
I am going to suggest strongly that we can get as much money as we like, we can organize a good army, and we may be one hundred per cent competent in that field, but in the final analysis the machinery of production in the country is just as necessary as any other phase of our military operations. Unless that is up to date and functioning perfectly, we are not going to get very far. I would suggest to the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Trade and Commerce-it is no one's particular job; it is everyone's job-that one of the first things that should be done is to bring the basic industries of this country under the national labour code. We had to do it during the last war, and we should do it again. The enemy is communism, and its agents are in this country. I never believed that the communists could hurt us in any sector of our society except the basic industries. If they get in there and sabotage them overnight, as they have in France and other countries, there is not much the government can do about it.
I believe that coal, steel, the railways are under it now; shipping, the packinghouse workers and auto workers should be brought under the national labour code. I also believe the government should take immediate steps to form industrial councils in those industries. There is such a council now in the building industry, and it functions well. The representatives from the unions, the employers, and the government could sit down now, when production is being planned, and help plan that production. In that way you send back to the unions, and the workers in the plant, liaison workers who can tell the people exactly what is taking place. You have an advocate on the inside. It is suspicion and fear that breed most of the unrest. Boards of directors trust their representatives, and the unions trust their representatives. If the representative of a union can return and say that this has been done and that has been done, and this is why it has 69262-22J
Defence Appropriation Act been done, it is a great help. You are making them partners in this plan to fight communism. In my opinion that is one of the best things that can be done-to get the basic industries tied up to the Department of Labour in planning this whole affair now so that the workers will have a share of the responsibility.
I do not believe it would be hard to do this. It is not a new idea, because the pattern was set by the federal Department of Labour during the last war, and even before that so far as the building trades are concerned. The building trades have their council, and they go to the Minister of Labour or his officials and work out their problems. As a result one seldom hears of any difficulty in that particular industry. I believe that should be done while this planning is being carried out. Through letters and discussion with the people who are affected, I know the people want that sort of thing. I do not want to start reading letters mentioning names, but that is one of the things you should start to do now.
I thought, Mr. Chairman, I should make these few remarks because of the trend the discussion has taken about planning for our defence. I do not think that kind of planning can be done here, but it can be done around a table. I know I sat on the last defence committee with the hon. member for Nanaimo, and I had no difficulty in getting along with him. He was just the member for Nanaimo expressing common-sense opinions about what was happening. I was greatly impressed by the representatives of the services, the navy, army and air force. They had men there who could allay all the suspicions and misapprehensions with regard to clauses about which I would have fought for weeks on the floor of the house. With people who knew and were able to give answers, my suspicions were removed without any difficulty. The same thing applies to this matter of defence. We are wondering now, and we do not know. We are voicing suspicions, and they are creating more suspicion outside. It is doing an injury to the very thing we want done.
It is my belief that the minister was ill advised in trying to answer questions this morning about the size of the army. I cannot see that in relation to these particular estimates. They represent getting some place to put the army, if and when we raise it, and to put some clothes on the men-things of that sort. The question raised by the member for Nanaimo as to the size of the army should be answered, but not here. I am not going to lecture the minister, but I do not think he should answer that sort

Defence Appropriation Act of thing in the house. Personally I should like such answers given in committee. When I go back to the people I represent, I should like to be able to tell them definitely just what the government proposes, and that I think that is necessary and right in view of the present international situation. I should like to be able to take my responsibility as a citizen, confident the government is doing everything they can in this situation. I cannot do that if I am frustrated, if I do not know and do not understand what is being done. I hate to express an opinion either for or against the government to anyone unless I am absolutely sure of what I am saying. I believe that committee should be set up as soon as possible, and put to work-not while the house is sitting; I think it is a little too serious for that. If necessary the committee should be here all the time, sitting with the defence department heads and the minister and helping them as best they can.
We do not want any more Koreas. It is a complete demonstration of our stupidity. We want to be in a position if something like that happens somewhere else to walk in with men who are trained, who know what they are doing and what they are fighting for, and be able to stop that sort of thing immediately. This can be done only by those who have an understanding of what is happening and confidence in the people who are carrying the responsibility. It is too serious to be quibbling about it.	.
I suggest the minister should consult with the heads of the government, the defence department, and ask them what they think about taking in these other fellows. We are taxpayers. We are citizens, and we believe in fighting communism. We want to do the right thing, and we want to help. The only way that I can see in which members of this house can help is by sitting on a committee, not to help formulate policy but to give the government the benefit of their opinions. Those opinions could be discussed with the men who have the responsibility, and plans made accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member referred to the extremely unfortunate accident at Petawawa, which I deeply regret. It is being thoroughly investigated. From the reports so far made to me, there is no evidence of negligence on the part of anyone. So far it would appear that the accident was due to the premature explosion of a mortar bomb in the barrel, and this type of accident had not, so I am informed, occurred before in training in Canada since the end of the second world war. It was something which could not be anticipated, and it will remain


to be learned from the report of the inquiry what steps should be taken to prevent a similar occurrence in the future. In the meantime the use of that ammunition has been stopped.
The hon. member mentioned one other thing which I must say came to me with surprise. He said he had had letters from fathers of sons in the special force, saying that the food is bad, the barracks dirty, and so on. I have seen a great deal of our armed forces. I have talked with the men individually, and have also talked with others who have been at our camps. I must say that I have not had any such report from any source whatever. As I think the hon. members knows, such complaints, if there are any, are reported in the newspapers or by letter, but no such complaint has reached me. I shall, however, be glad to look into the matter, if the hon. member will hand to me the letter or give me the name of the place in question; and if any other hon. member knows of any such circumstances, if he will let me know, I shall be glad to look into them.
Our aim has been to give the men nothing but the best, and I think we have done fairly well in giving them adequate food, good clothing and good living conditions. If there is any failure in that respect, if hon. members will only let me know at once, I will have an immediate and thorough investigation made.

I have
already taken up the time of the house to express my views on the setting up of a committee, and for that reason alone I would hesitate to say more than a word on it. In addition I would hesitate to follow the most excellent remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, for fear of doing injustice to the topic. But I just want to say this, because it seems to me that somehow or other we are failing to reach common sense.

I am only saying that the speech, full of good sense, made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South I suggest affords the minister a chance to get away from this difficulty, this situation in which we now think he is giving us bits and pieces of information and not the comprehensive statement that we want.

Who would be on that committee? On that committee presumably would be men from various parties, with military experience themselves, whose loyalty would be unquestioned in any man's language.
The minister has another fear which we must meet. If I remember aright, he said yesterday that there will be exchanged beween governments secrets which cannot be disclosed. Does he think any of these men would press him and ask for the disclosure of something which he said should not be disclosed? Of course he does not think that. I therefore suggest again that we have that committee, where we shall be able to work together, and where the public of Canada will be convinced we are working together; otherwise we can go on with this fruitless waste of time, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South described it; and it will go on like that if this present situation is allowed to continue.

to give us a statement as to the housing provisions which are being made for married personnel? At the present time housing in urban centres is not contemplated for members of the armed forces, except in extremely unusual circumstances where it is found by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that there will be a continuing need for special accommodation for service personnel and where the supply of civilian quarters for them is going to be insufficient for a period as far ahead as one can see. Such a place is Rockcliffe, for example, where we have already constructed, I believe, 134 houses. Another 174 are under construction, and 300 more will be started as soon as possible.
In isolated centres our aim is to provide married quarters for all the married personnel that need them. That program has been pushed forward since 1947, so that with the houses already constructed or the construction of which has been approved, out of the appropriations for the current year, we shall have 10,773 married quarters for the personnel of the armed forces.
At some centres such as, for example, Goose Bay and Shilo, which have been given high priority, there are enough married quarters to accommodate all or almost all the
Defence Appropriation Act married personnel needing them. At other centres where there have been considerable changes in the strength of the establishment, such as Petawawa, although we have built there a great number of houses, we still need to build some more and we shall be pressing on with that. We shall be continuing the arrangement under which a large part of the building program for the Department of National Defence is carried out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and met out of their vote, although that will require an adjustment between the two departments later. The policy is for the Department of National Defence itself to-carry out the construction in isolated centres-such as Whitehorse, Churchill, Yellowknife,, and the like, where the costs are high and where Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation ordinarily have not facilities of inspection, service and the like.
That gives you the picture in general, terms. We have met the shortage to a considerable degree. We have put into three-years what was originally planned as a six-or seven-year program. It is being proceeded' with, however, and while at the present time we may continue to be limited by labour and materials, these can be met.

To some people this may seem to be a small matter, but the whole question of the morale of the reserve forces is important and should have serious consideration by the committee.
Not only do members of the reserve force have to pay income tax on the additional amounts they receive, but, as was pointed out this morning, this sometimes results in their being brought into a higher income tax bracket, and as a result the pay they receive may be partly wiped out. Secondly, is the government considering; means by which further monetary encouragement may be given to those who are doing such a magnificent job in our reserve forces? Defence Appropriation Act
I wonder if we do not take too much for granted the work done by those who are in the reserve forces. It is not a spectacular service, but parliament should take cognizance of what they have done in keeping the pilot light burning between wars. I agree with everything the hon. member has said. We have emphasized the importance of the reserve army and the grand job they are doing. As I have told the house' on several occasions, the question of exemptions from income tax for the pay and allowances for reserve officers and men has been taken up a number of times. I believe I said formerly that the amount involved in government revenue is negligible, while the amount involved in nuisance is very considerable. From the point of view of greater interest in the reserve forces, I should be very glad personally to see some method worked out by which the pay and allowances of members of the reserve navy, army, and air force might in some way be exempt from income tax.
The general principle which the government has adopted, and which I think has met with general agreement, is that everything in the nature of income should be subject to taxation. I have indicated to representatives of the reserve associations and to hon. members on a number of occasions that if they or we could find some formula which would do the required jotb, other than an outright statutory exemption, I would certainly be glad to take it up with my colleagues the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue. We have had officers in the department and outside accountants in the reserve forces consider various proposals, but so far one has not yet been put forward. It would appear that if this were to be done it would have to be by an amendment to the Income Tax Act. So far the government has not been prepared to accept that. I can assure the hon. member for Peel and all others that any way in which the fine and unselfish services of the officers of the reserve force can be properly recognized in a monetary fashion certainly will receive every possible consideration.
Since the change in the pay rates adopted in 1946 we have put the reserve and active forces on exactly the same basis with regard to pay and allowances and conditions of ser-
[Mr. Graydon.j

vice, and we think it rather important that that similarity should be maintained. If hon. members can make any constructive suggestions as to what should be done along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Peel, we shall be only too glad to accept them. I can assure the hon. member that the matter is receiving active consideration.

The reserve army is on a part-time basis, and I think "part-time" might be underlined and underscored. Because it is on a part-time basis, the dislocation which takes place in their civilian life is considerable. Surely in these times, when there is such a great need for reserve army personnel, the minister might consider some arrangement by which they could be paid an additional amount by virtue of the temporary or parttime character of their duties. As the minister knows, in civilian life part-time work commands a higher rate of pay than work on a weekly, monthly or yearly basis. I am not suggesting for one moment, and I fancy no one would, that the question of dollars and cents enters into this question of reserve army training. The naked fact is that a good many men lose money through taking an active part in this training. It has been a losing proposition for many thousands of them, and I do not think we ought to compel them to lose money when they carry out their patriotic duty as they see it.
There is real need of indicating in some way that we do appreciate the work these patriotic men are doing. At times it is not particularly spectacular; there is considerable slogging to do, but these men are working hard in an effort to provide security for the rest of us in Canada through a peacetime period.

Just before the luncheon recess this committee had the privilege of listening to one of the most constructive and sensible speeches I have heard since I came to this house. I refer to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I do not think anyone will contend that that hon. member was partisan. We were impressed by the suggestion he made, a suggestion which has been made by other members of the opposition, that a defence committee should be set up. As he pointed out, this debate is apt to go on for a long time.
The government seem to feel that if they accept any suggestion of the opposition they are in some way losing prestige, and the result is that the opposition have to go ahead and do the best they can to pry out answers. As the hon. member said this morning, I do not think that that is a constructive way of getting on with the vitally important business of this house. It would be a fine gesture on the part of the government if they could accept the sincere suggestion made this morning. It would raise them in the estimation of the people if once in a while they could give way to the unanimous opinion of the opposition. In the meantime until that committee is established, if it ever is, we must continue to try to get information by asking perhaps interminable questions.
Possibly I am in a slightly better position to understand the problems of the reserve army than some members of the house, because I happen to be a member of it at the present time. But I must say that I have learned absolutely nothing so far about our plans for preparing this country to defend itself in any eventuality. I have tried to understand. I have conscientiously listened to everything that has been said, and I am as much at sea now as I was when I came to the house over a week ago.
This morning the Minister of National Defence told us that in his opinion, and in the opinion of his department, we do not need a division to provide for the protection of Canada. He said that a brigade group could adequately defend our vast area. We have also learned that the brigade group has a dual task. It has the task of training further forces which might be raised for service elsewhere. I do not believe that it can remain in a state of readiness to act as a formation and at the same time be spread over several

Defence Appropriation Act training areas training other people. I just do not think it can be done. Let us suppose for a moment, however, that it can be done. When would the brigade group be ready to act as a formation and fight as a brigade? To get some information on that point I asked the hon. member for Nanaimo the same question this morning. I think all hon. members will agree that he is one of the foremost Canadian military authorities today; and he said he believed that it would take probably two months from today, if preparations were started at once, before the formation could fight as a brigade group.
The first question I want to ask the minister is when the brigade group will be ready to fight as a brigade. Then I want to deal with the creation of further forces. With the world situation as it is today I do not think there is a doubt in any hon. member's mind that the creation of the Korean brigade is not the last troop formation we shall have to raise. We have obligations under the United Nations organization and as a member of the North Atlantic pact. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us last June when he came back from a meeting of the Atlantic pact countries, the cardinal principle laid down at that meeting was that in future no build-up of forces would be permitted behind a bulwark of overrun nations. In other words, members of the North Atlantic pact who are expected to supply forces against aggression in the future must have those forces ready.
We are told that the role of the permanent force will be to stay in Canada for the purpose of training and preparing forces which may be used either in Canada or in other parts of the world. Therefore if we are called upon to raise other forces it will require a minimum of six to eight months, as has been required to raise the Korean brigade. Under the plan that I submitted to the Minister of National Defence we would at all times have a division trained and ready, and maintained at a minimum of cost to the taxpayers. The minister does not regard that as a good idea. Therefore as my second question I am going to ask him whether we are planning on a requirement of six to eight months each time we are called upon to produce armed forces to fulfil our obligations to the United Nations and as a member of the North Atlantic pact.
The third subject I want to deal with is the reserve army. Any member of the reserve forces will tell you that it would require a minimum of nine months to one year before a reserve division would be ready to fight as a formation. What I want to find out is

Mr. Chairman, answering the hon. member's questions in reverse order, I must say that the figures do not bear out his last remark about the lack of results of recruiting efforts for the reserve forces. In January, 1948, the strength of the Canadian army reserve was 33,369, and in July, 1950, it was 44,314, an increase of over thirty per cent. Furthermore, the proportion that is effective and is taking full training has increased to an even greater degree, as was indicated by the hon. member for Westmorland in the figures he gave to the house. Therefore I simply do not agree with this policy of despair so far as our reserve forces are concerned. They are doing a great job. I think, given encouragement and help in every way that we can give it, they will continue to recruit at a rate that will enable them to build up to the standards we are aiming at for them, which are equivalent to those of active force troops. That standard has been virtually achieved in the case of a relatively small number of units, but it indicates that it can be done.
When we entered the first great war and the second great war it was largely on the basis of the reserve army that the forces were built up. That is still the plan, but it can be done now very much faster because the forces are to a greater extent more effective, and have a greater number of officers who are physically fit and qualified, as well as N.C.O.'s and tradesmen. It can also be done very much faster because we have the equipment with which to supply them for training purposes, and also, as I indicated before, equipment that would to a considerable degree be sufficient for the Canadian army during the first year in a total war. So the situation is entirely different from what it was between the wars or before the first war; but, granted further co-operation, this challenging question can be met, and I am sure will be met, by added support for the reserve forces. If, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Peel, there are ways in which greater incentive can be given, then let us have them and consider them.
As to the suggestion of the hon. member that the role of the permanent force is to

stay here and train, some 'Clarification must be given. The permanent force army does not consist only of the brigade group; it includes all the officers and men at headquarters engaged in administrative and training work, those attached to reserve army units, the engineers, R.C.E.M.E. and so on, equipped and trained to do the job of organizing and getting going. It also includes complete machinery for training officers, N.C.O.'s and men at the schools now in operation for the training of active force and reserve army personnel. In those training staffs we have large numbers of men-more than in the brigade group- engaged full-time, who would be carrying on that training in the event of an emergency.
At the present time the brigade group itself is not only doing its job of being available for the defence of Canada; it is also helping to train the special force. So far as one can see, while the one operation may interfere a little with the other, the brigade group is carrying on both tasks, which I suggest is inevitable in the case of any regular and reserve army. The regulars must carry out the dual function of being available for immediate defence and assisting in training. If the threat of immediate attack on Canada should disappear and be known not to exist to the same extent that had been feared, then of course in an emergency the brigade group of the active force would be available at once for service abroad. It would also be available as other men were trained to take its place. So the suggestion that the permanent force is a stay-at-home army is totally false and entirely out of accord with our announced plans.
As to the time it would take to train a unit, of course this would depend upon the state of training of the unit at the time the period of intense training began, and various other conditions existing at the time. It would' be quite possible for the brigade group to get into action very rapidly, indeed' in far less time than two months; but I must admit that I entirely agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo that this would not be desirable, and that two months would be a reasonable period for them to have, if that were possible. If it were not, then the brigade group could get into action sooner.

When we started this discussion in committee I understood that hon. members were going to be permitted to make general observations on what might be called item No. 1, and that questions then would come on the various items in the schedules. Some of us have been sitting here for some time waiting to say a word or two. I am not going to speak at length. I am not capable of speaking of such broad military considerations as have been dealt with by the member for Nanaimo, or by our military expert the member for Cape Breton South. But I do want to make a few-observations that come to me as a result of reading this resolution, knowing the situation in the country and having some faint idea of what the average person thinks about problems of this sort. This unexpected and additional expense will place extra burdens on the Canadian people, an unavoidable burden in taxes, and possibly a burden in rising prices and shortages.
We in this group, Mr. Chairman, support the contention of the official opposition that in order to assure sound economy at this time, and to get the greatest co-operation in the country, there should be a committee on defence. I do not think many members in this house, with the exception of one or two, are capable of discussing military problems on a broad scale, or wish to have, shall I say, secret matters brought to the attention of this house. The great majority of the members of this house, however, are capable of discussing the procedures in expenditures, costs, contracts and things of that sort, which we believe could be discussed by a defence committee to great advantage. In this way the opposition members could secure information they desire and also assist the minister.
Military expenditures are somewhat more difficult to check than expenditures by other government departments. If the Department of Public Works, for instance, builds a wharf or erects a building, we have concrete evidence of the expenditure in a form that the average person can understand. Military expenditures are somewhat different. It is because of that difference between military and civil expenditures and, shall I


say, the intangible nature of military expenditures on occasions, that we believe it is more necessary than ever for this house to have a defence committee.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that public opinion at this time will demand that this government secure good value for its expenditures on national defence. In saying that I am thinking of a few things that I noticed during the last war. Unfortunately when you reach a period of expansion in the defence services you have in some quarters a sense of irresponsibility. You have a core of responsible and practical officers in your defence department, but inevitably, as a result of the expansion of the services, there is also the possibility of getting some personnel who are not responsible. I remember during the last war going from Vancouver to the interior of British Columbia on a train with a senior military officer. On the train he had a drawing room and all the extra comforts of life, to go with it. Upon arriving at a small town where he had to leave the main line and take a local train a distance of twenty miles, he discovered that the local train had no sleeper, no drawing room and no chair car. His passage had been paid by the people of Canada from Vancouver to the point to which he was going. The conductor said, "Sir, you will have to ride in the day coach". The senior military officer said, "I am not riding in any day coach". What did he do? He telephoned for a car to come for him and carry him to the end of his journey. This meant that a car travelled forty miles at public expense because this high and mighty person would not travel in a day coach with such lowly people as myself and other local people.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that sort of thing is not good for the morale of the people of Canada. The conductor on the train, the train crew, and all the passengers in the coach witnessed or heard of this situation with disgust. I just bring that forward as one illustration of the irresponsible approach to the expenditure of public funds on one occasion.
I want to mention now the question of military cars and military vehicles. I am quite sure the minister will do what he can to check this type of irresponsibility at this time. I am not saying it is happening now, but I am just giving my experiences. We all know there has always been a tendency in the past for members of the armed forces, particularly senior commissioned officers, to consider themselves as almost a caste apart from ordinary human beings. They consider it the prerogative of the colonel to have the chauffeur drive his wife to pink teas, and

things of that sort. I hope that sort of thing will not be allowed under these conditions. Mrs. Muggins will not think much of that sort of thing if she finds she is helping to pay through taxation for the transportation of the colonel's wife to a pink tea.

On another occasion I saw a large army truck loaded with equipment, blankets, bedding and that sort of thing. I said, "What is going on here?" I discovered that some of the officers were going on a hunting trip for the week end with this large truck, chauffeur, and gasoline all paid for by the public. I hope the minister will see that that sort of thing does not happen under present circumstances. I just mention these few instances. No doubt they are violations of the regulations, and so on, but if this is to be a democratic effort; if we are to have the co-operation of most of the people, they must be shown that the department receives value for the money spent. These are only a few illustrations on a small scale, but to the average person they are indications of a wasteful approach to the expenditure of public money. I do hope that the minister exercises the strictest supervision in this respect, and issues instructions that this sort of thing shall not occur, because this money is being paid with some difficulty by many Canadian people.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned that he had heard the food was not good in some of the camps. I have heard, quite recently and almost directly, that the situation at Petawawa is not satisfactory so far as food is concerned. I am not certain of my information, but I am informed that the contractors for the reserve army are now cooking for the special forces and there is considerable dissatisfaction. I could give the minister a number of other illustrations, but I am not going to take the time of the committee. I do urge the minister to give serious consideration to these small aspects of expenditure in order to prove to the Canadian people that the large expenditures are being given serious consideration. As I said before, small as they are, they indicate to the public a wasteful approach to the expenditure of money by the Department of National Defence.
