In this group we believe that if we are going to do that, in view of the increasing burden on the people of this country it is necessary for this government to make every effort to protect the living standards of the people. Without question prices have not risen since the Korean incident as a result of increased wages. They have risen for two reasons. The first reason is outright greed, and the second is fear of shortages. I do hope the government does something to protect the Canadian public before this session is over. There is a rising demand in Canada for the reimposition of price controls and necessary subsidies. Trade unions are urging this action, and consumers' groups are expressing their opinions very strongly. Only in this morning's Citizen I read that the executive council of the Canadian Legion in Quebec intend to bring before the national convention of the Canadian Legion a resolution urging the reimposition by this government of necessary price controls. In addition to that, a good number of smaller businessmen who at one time joined the uniholy chorus of decontrol-who had written to me or come to me and spoken to me and said that they wanted controls taken off; they sincerely felt that it would permit them to operate to greater advantage-these men are coming back now and saying: For heaven's sake let us have some control over this economy so that we shall know where we are; we were better off-and I am speaking of friends I have in the lumber and other industries-with price control, than we are now with this unstable price condition.
In conclusion I therefore urge again that this government give consideration to the establishment of a defence committee to work as outlined by several previous speakers, with a view to ensuring wise economy in the expenditures for the defence of this country; and in securing that wise economy to secure the broad-based support of the Canadian people. Mr. Chairman, the arguments and the criticisms which I am going to put forward are based on the premise that we are facing a genuine and real emergency, the full extent of which is perhaps not realized by all our people, and that we face certain disaster if we do not act now to an even greater extent than has been outlined in the program put forward by the government to meet that crisis.
I am supported in this position by statements made by the Prime Minister and the

Defence Appropriation Act Secretary of State for External Affairs particularly, and by others on the government side, particularly the hon. member for Port-neuf, who spoke yesterday morning. In addition to those statements the whole premise that we are facing a catastrophe is, I think, strongly supported by the present turn of events in Korea.
Just the other day the Prime Minister told us that in ten months we might be brought face to face with a war. It was not just the possibility of another isolated aggression; that was not the meaning of the Prime Minister's words. It is true he said that if we escaped a war for the next ten months, we might then begin to be able to hope for peace. The only meaning which could be taken from his words, in the context in which he used them, is that there is real danger of a war in the next ten months.
Then there is the Korean situation, and we must remember all that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has told us-that any aggressor who finds that he can get away with one aggression is encouraged and proceeds at an increasingly rapid pace from one aggression to another. We agree with that view. I therefore think that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree with me when I say that if the present trend of events in Korea comes to the disastrous conclusion which unfortunately at the moment it seems to be pointing to, namely, a defeat for the United Nations forces, the international situation will be infinitely worsened.
All the spokesmen from the government side, supported by everyone else who has spoken in this chamber, have outlined Canada's duty to take her part to meet this aggression, to play her role as one of the United Nations in preserving peace. I am therefore not going to enlarge upon what they have said. It is obvious that all members of the House of Commons, as well as, I believe, everyone throughout the country- except perhaps the few communists we may have in Canada-support that position and fully agree that this time we must learn the lessons of the past and act before it is too late. We must meet this threat. I believe that any proper action taken to prepare ourselves not only to meet the threat but to discourage an aggressor by positive readiness will be wholeheartedly supported from one end of Canada to the other. Based upon that argument, my criticism is that we are not doing sufficient to meet this situation.
In the first place, an analysis of our defence position indicates that we are not getting value for our money. It is true that this year we are intending to spend a large sum, $1,400 million. But if we compare the return that

we are getting for the money which we are being asked to spend this year with what we got for what we spent on the same basis during the war years, we can see immediately that the comparison is most unfavourable and indicates that we are not getting value for that money.
During the war years our war expenditures reached a peak in the year 1943. If hon. members will look at the table presented by the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, appearing at page 392 of Hansard of February 11, 1944, they will see that in 1943-44 we spent $3,824 million on defence. In 1944-45 we spent $3,619 million on defence. Those were the total expenditures of the government attributable to defence purposes. This year we are spending on the defence of Canada over one-third of the amount which we spent during the peak year of the last war.
If one looks at the actual war effort, the peak effort Canada was putting forward at that time, measured by the most immediately available measure to hand1-that is, the number of men under arms-one finds that the peak of all three services was approximately
780.000	men and women. That is the maximum number that we had under arms at any one time. As close as one can come to it, Mr. Chairman, that peak was reached in the year 1943. It is true that the navy reached its peak in 1944; but both the army and the air force reached their peaks in 1943. The maximum number under arms was 780,000. At the present time, according to the figures which have been produced by the minister, we have for the three permanent forces a ceiling which has recently been raised to 69,160.
The other day the minister told us that the actual strength is 56,962. There are some
60.000	men in the reserve forces; so we have a total of about 120,000 men, of whom half are reserve. But even including the reserve forces we have only about one-seventh the number of men in the services for one-third the total expenditures of the war years. Or, taking the minister's figures, which I do not admit to be correct, he makes the expenditure about one-seventh. That gives us the figure of one-fifteenth the number of men for an expenditure of one-seventh the amount of money.
It is seen, therefore, that an examination of the figures with a view to comparing the relative efforts indicates clearly that we are not getting value for our defence dollar today as compared with the value we received for it in the 1939-45 war.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has just referred to the tendency toward relaxation of the control of expenditures during
Defence Appropriation Act wartime. I am not going to say that that is completely correct, but it certainly must be remembered that during a war the main effort is to win the war. There is, shall I say, less rigid control of expenditures for that purpose than there is supposed to be during a normal period of peace. This year-at least up to the present-we were supposed to be back to peacetime rigidity and economy of expenditures. Certainly all the ministers have insisted that there is not one cent of extravagance or duplication. That being so, it reinforces the argument that on the basis of comparative expenditures and comparative returns we are not getting value for our defence dollar.
I put forward next the criticism that to a large extent what is happening in the outline of government policy is that we are talking but not acting. We have so-called plans laid before us with respect to the increase of ceilings and the recruiting program, but we are not given any definite date at which it is expected those programs will have been fulfilled.
This afternoon as well as this morning, politely it is true but quite firmly, the minister refused to say when we might expect our forces to be ready. The situation in this regard is I think not new in any country. I could not help doing some studying to find a parallel situation, and I think I have found one which pretty well parallels that which faces us today. It is found in the words of a statesman of a good many thousand years ago.
Only the other day the hon. member for Greenwood described the activities of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when forces were sought by the United Nations for service in Korea, and what happened between that time and the time the government came to its decision. The hon. member described the Secretary of . State for External Affairs as hurrying back and forth to conferences, and the simile he drew was perfectly accurate. I have here the words of an orator who spoke several hundred years before Christ, when his country was faced with a similar situation, and they are certainly applicable at this time. This is what he said:
But look to this, Athenians, that our envoys shall not only make speeches, but have some real proof that we have gone forth as becomes our country, and are engaged in action. All speech without action appears vain and idle, but especially that of our commonwealth; as the more we are thought to excel therein, the more is our speaking distrusted by all. You must show yourselves, greatly reformed, greatly changed, contributing, serving personally, acting promptly, before anyone will pay attention to you.

Another thing, too, you should observe, Athenians, that a decree is worth nothing without a readiness on your part to do what you determine. Some say that it is untimely and unpatriotic to mention the problem of manpower at this time, but I do not think it is. This problem has arisen before, and the refusal to recognize its existence in time created more harm throughout Canada than could possibly have been created had the problem been dealt with in time. There are hon. members who were here in the period from 1939 to 1945 who will remember the damage caused to national unity by the refusal to deal with this problem until it was too late to do so impartially and fairly.
All I am suggesting is that when we are faced with a threat to our very existence as a nation we ought not to close our minds to the fact that this is a problem to be faced, nor should we blind ourselves to the fact that the protection of the national security of Canada is the duty and obligation of every Canadian. That national obligation should be distributed fairly and with justice among all the individuals in our society. In my view this can be done only if we enact legislation now which would distribute the burden fairly among all our citizens. Then when the time comes we could invoke that legislation.

One of the disadvantages of a debate of this kind is that it is not very coherent in that we have no definite clause before us to follow. The debate wanders around from subject to subject in accordance with the will of the speaker in each case. We have had a matter of tremendous importance put before us by the hon. member for Kamloops. Perhaps it will be somewhat of a let-down if I proceed to discuss a comparatively trivial matter, although I do not think it i9 particularly trivial.
My remarks might have followed better those of my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, or perhaps even those of the hon. member for Peel who spoke some time ago about how some people were mulcted even for their patriotic efforts. The hon. member for Kootenay West said that public moneys are sometimes squandered in the case of military expenditures. The hon. member for Kamloops spoke about the conscription of men. I hope to say a word or two about what is virtually conscription of funds in time of war, and the result of it, so far as the people whose money is so used are concerned. In other words, I want tc say a word about the effect that the injection of these tremendous sums of money into the economy of our country, already feverish and inflated, will have.
By its very nature this must act as a stimulus, in an economy already inflated to the danger point, to prices already much too high. I think the government will have to devise some means of checking this inflation. Much has been said, perhaps mainly by those of this group but also by those in other quarters of the house where people may still be vocal, of the hardships which have been endured by the people of this country up to the present. Those on low and indeed on moderate incomes have been compelled to reduce their standards of living. The low purchasing power of money has weighed heavily on those with fixed incomes, such as military pensioners, civil servants, old age pensioners and the like. Many people in what are often called humble positions have been forced to use

their savings to meet the exigencies of the moment; this has been brought to my attention by many of my acquaintances. In some cases they have even given up their life insurance, and of course the selling of war bonds in order to get some ready cash is a common practice. It has become more and more difficult for wage earners to stretch their wages to meet the increased cost of the necessities of family life. In 1948 the royal commission on prices stated it was probable that most workers were as well off then as they were in 1945. That may have been true at that time, though you will notice it was not made as a definite assertion; but I doubt whether the rise in wages since that date has kept pace with the increased cost of living. I suggest that now prices have outstripped wages and salaries. Certainly that is so in the case of the people about whom I have been talking, the widows, those drawing veterans' allowance, those on pension, and so on.
I suppose what I have said refers largely to urban communities, but the same situation exists throughout the rural communities as well, because of the tremendous increase in the costs of production on the farm. Farmers have been worried about this tremendous increase in prices; and may I say that in my opinion many of these increases, which have been progressively greater since the beginning of the Korean trouble, were not at all justified. We have the instance of the increase in the price of sugar, though it was shown that we have greater stocks of sugar in the world today than ever before. Farmers have been paying higher prices for their machinery. When you meet a farmer on the road in Saskatchewan today with a combine on his truck and ask what he paid for it, it is not unusual to be told that the price was in the neighbourhood of $5,000; and there have been increases in the cost of oil, twine and repairs.
Organized farmers, of course, are doing something about this. It is this increase in prices that has caused renewed activity on the part of the farmers' union in the province of Saskatchewan. They have come to realize, I believe, that their cause is somewhat the same as that of labour; in fact they have acknowledged this in their speeches and pamphlets. They are asking for an adjustment, for some control of prices, at least on a parity basis; and I hope the government will see fit to do something to bring about such an equitable parity. If we are to judge from the history of the past, however, the government will avoid that; but certainly it must introduce some anti-inflationary
Defence Appropriation Act measures in order to control expenditures. I suppose we might predict higher income taxes and perhaps an excess profits tax.
Now I come to the point I particularly wanted to make today. I believe there should be some domestic financing in order to draw off some of the extra money that has been accruing to at least some sections of the population during these periods of war and rumours of war. If the government cannot give the assurance of some degree of stability in the price structure over a period of years, it may have difficulty in its domestic financing in peacetime, when the purchase of government bonds is not stimulated by the patriotic feeling prevalent in time of war. There is no doubt that this patriotic motive does encourage the almost universal purchase of war bonds during times of national emergency.
It would be rather interesting to look into this question of bonds. I do not know much about them, but like many others I thought it my duty to invest in a bond or two of small denomination during the war. This morning I looked up the figures in the Canada Year Book, and I find that the price of bonds has varied very little, ranging from $100 to $104. After support was withdrawn a year or two ago the price went back to about $102, and I should imagine that the average would be below that figure. Those bonds, of course, had a par value of $100. Then I looked up the cost of living index during the same period. Taking 1939 as 100 I found that in 1945 the index was 119; in 1947 it was 144; in 1948 it was 159; in 1949 it was 160-8, and for the month of August, 1950-of course we have not the figure for the year yet-it was 168-5, the highest in our history. When we come to the index figure for food-and may I say that in- these days, when wages have to be stretched to cover the necessities of life, the greater part of those wages must be spent on food-we find that the figure is 216-7.
My point is that if a person invested $100 in a war bond in 1942 or thereabouts and sold that bond today, he would get somewhere between $100 and $102 for it; but if he took that money into a store he would be able to purchase food worth only about $50 on the basis of prices in 1942. In other words, even adding the interest received in the meantime, the amount received for the bond today would not nearly equal in purchasing power the amount of money originally invested. Thus when the government urges us to invest in these bonds as a patriotic duty, we certainly do just that; we perform an unselfish, patriotic duty not only in

Defence Appropriation Act lending but in giving the government money for the purpose of war expenditures.
This is a point I thought should be drawn to the attention of this house. Even children appreciate it. I heard of one instance in a family somewhat connected with my own, only the other day. A little girl had a war savings certificate. Her parents had paid only $4 for it; now she got $5; but even that young girl had sufficient acumen to realize that when she spent that money she did not get anything like what $4 would have bought at the time the war savings certificate was purchased for her. I want to draw that to the attention of the government. I suppose it is a small thing, but it is generally felt throughout the whole population.
In so far as these great expenditures proposed are concerned, we realize they are a necessity at this time. I think I can say we shall support the government in the expenditure of these moneys. Looking out in the world today we come to the conclusion that we must be strong. We would need to be strong to maintain neutrality as between combatants in whose combat we were not particularly interested. By that strength we might be able to maintain that position of neutrality. By that strength we would serve notice to the combatants that they had better not violate such neutrality or make our country a battleground. Having said that, I must go on to say that we think we must be strong in order that we may fulfil our commitments to the United Nations in putting down aggression wherever it may occur. We must be strong in order to fulfil our commitments to those to whom we would naturally look for assistance in our defence.
I believe the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) took a somewhat unrealistic attitude. Although he sits on the Conservative benches his opinions appear to be different from those of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), who has just spoken in this debate. The hon. member for Labelle is living in a world of unreality if he imagines that we can possibly defend our shores against all comers. Does he not realize that there are mighty nations in this world against whom we could not hope to stand alone? How could we expect other nations to come to our defence if we did not reciprocate and fulfil our commitments to those nations? I believe that is all I wish to say upon the matter. For these reasons, although we abhor war, we shall be prepared to support the resolution, even to the extent of these colossal sums of money.

Our commitment under the United Nations charter in regard to the supplying of military forces to carry out our obligations is therefore exactly the same as the commitment of Brazil, South Africa, the United States or any other member, namely to do our best to carry out the recommendations of assistance made by a United Nations agency, which we have agreed to do.
How we will do that has not been worked out under the charter. As the agreements under article 43 have been shown to be impossible because of the attitude of the U.S.S.R., I hope that we may work this out in a different way, possibly starting at this forthcoming assembly, and in a way which the U.S.S.R. will not be able to prevent. For that purpose the precedent-and I think it is a precedent which we have established-of earmarking our military forces for carrying out UN commitments may be followed by the same kind of procedure in other countries, so that we shall have the beginning of a United Nations force, national contingents, earmarked to carry out specifically certain obligations. That is, however, in the future.
As to the commitment under the North Atlantic pact, as my colleague has stated, we have a general commitment to do what we can to meet an aggression on any member of the group. That is our political commitment and we must live up to it. How we carry out that political commitment in military terms is something that is being worked out now by the appropriate agencies under the North Atlantic council.
The discussions of this matter were going on last spring when I attended the meeting of the North Atlantic council, and there were being negotiated by the military experts of the North Atlantic agencies various arrangements which would have provided certain detailed plans so that each member of the group would know what its military commitment was in case a political commitment was engaged. Defence Appropriation Act been modified in the course of the discussions this summer so that they will be made rather broader, and deeper in character, and will be brought into effect more speedily.

The North Atlantic council deputies on Saturday adjourned their meetings until 13th September, 1950, when they will convene in New York prior to the meeting of the North Atlantic council.
The council deputies drew up plans to Implement and finance a priority production program, and recommended to their governments the immediate placing of orders, up to the full utilization of existing capacity, for certain specified items of equipment most urgently required for the forces contemplated under approved defence plans. This priority program will be embodied in future long-term plans for the production and financing of military equipment.
The deputies inaugurated an urgent study, with the assistance of the appropriate agencies of the North Atlantic treaty, of the measures required, first, to strengthen the military organization of the treaty, and, second, to decide what arrangements would bring about a fair distribution of the financial burden and the most effective and economic use of the collective resources of the twelve countries for the defence of the North Atlantic area.

what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said; but what he has said has underlined the necessity of parliament and the people of Canada finding out what the major nature of our contribution is to be under the North Atlantic pact.
In July the United Nations World dealt with the situation generally with regard to Canada's contribution. Among other things it said this, and I am reading from an article by the editor:	-
For too long Canada has been overlooked when the North American potential for peace or war was being estimated. The resources and potentials of the United States have monopolized the spotlight, for indeed the U.S. achievement is spectacular.
Then it goes on to say about Canada:
Apart from giving credit where credit is due, nobody can think accurately about the North American continent unless he adds Canada's assets to those of the United States.
Canada is the second largest country in the world, since the USSR began whittling off pieces of China . . .
The old word "inexhaustible," can be dusted off and used again for the mineral wealth of Canada. The possibilities have only been tapped but already the list includes gold, silver, copper, nickel, platinum, uranium, radium, cobalt, cadmium, tungsten, magnesium, mercury, asbestos, oil, iron and coal.
In the United Nations World it is set out that there must be mobilization of both manpower and material resources of the nations making up the North Atlantic pact. It is a matter of surprise that at this late date the minister is still in a position where, in effect, he says that there has been no decision as to the responsibility of the several countries making up the pact.
It was for that reason that I asked the question the other day as to Canada's objective. What are the plans of the government? Is our contribution to the prevention of aggression to be manpower, or is it to be industrial expansion, or is it to be the development of our natural resources? Certainly when one reads the article that was published three years ago in the Saturday Evening Post one has cause to think. At that time Mr. Averell Harriman, secretary of commerce in the United States, speaking about the United States, said:
Having ruthlessly tapped our natural resources, we are becoming a "have-not nation."
The United States has the industrial capacity for expansion. In the last war Canada made tremendous advances in this connection, too; but we have in addition the needs without which the war potential of Canada and of all the nations in 'the North Atlantic pact cannot achieve the maximum.

As I have said on previous occasions, I believe the time has come for an announcement from the government as to what Canada's contribution is to be. Certainly, having regard to the fact that our armed forces are to be kept to a minimum, and having regard to the international situation, the question which naturally suggests itself is this: Has it been agreed that in place of manpower Canada's contribution is going to be expanded mineral development, expanded development of those things that are as yet hidden in the ground, but potentially available and requiring only development? It was because of that fact that I suggested that, the natural resources and their administration being within the prerogative of the provinces, when the dominion-provincial conference meets a plan should be arrived at whereby, in co-operation, there will be an intensified and accelerated development in the expansion of our resources, particularly our iron, oil and coal, and such other minerals as are required in the development of this nation.
We ask questions and we get such information as the government vouchsafes us, and believes it is proper that we should have. But no one in the House of Commons-indeed, now we can say no one in parliament, because the minister says there is no over-all plan in the mind of the government or the nations making up the North Atlantic pact-knows what each one of these nations is to produce or to provide in the event of aggression.
I believe the government would go a long way if it were to say to the people either that their responsibility is going to be one of manpower, despite a comparatively small population of some 14 million people or, on the other hand, their main contribution to the resistance of aggression will be the provision of the resources they have and without which there could not be mobilization for defence or total war. Never have we had a greater opportunity in that direction.
In my own province of Saskatchewan the potential development of oil has blanketed the province with oil rights owned and controlled by Americans who have come to this country. We have had these potential resources, and yet Canadians have not been developing them. Are these resources now to be developed? What co-operation is there to be, and what is going to be done to the end that the United States, with its vast industrial opportunities, will have those resources available to it in the event that aggression does strike North America or any of the other countries making up the North Atlantic pact? What provision will there be for the mobilization of these resources?
Defence Appropriation Act
This is a matter upon which all of us want information, and upon which hon. members individually can determine their attitude toward the whole question of manpower and the necessity for the provision of manpower for the preservation of our way of life. I trust it will not be long before the government will be in a position to make a statement in this particular. They were asked the question in 1945-and I have the debates here-"When are you going to arrive at some conclusion?"
Well, the United Nations has been emasculated by the overhanging veto in the hands of the five powers, and used in particular by one of them.

What is this operation to be? Is it to be merely a palatable one; is it to be a manpower one; is it to be an industrial one? If it is to be a manpower one, then certain questions arise. If it is to consist of the development of our resources, to provide for the have-not nations those natural resources we have here in abundance as yet undeveloped, then we in this country should know, so that we would be in a position to meet the challenge. The Prime Minister has said that within a decade of months-and those were striking words-we may find ourselves with our way of life challenged. Surely we do not meet the possible challenge in a decade of months by the announcement made this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence that what we now vote in money to a great extent will not be expended for two years, or even beyond that.

speechtext:
I think in the interests of the Canadian people and also of the other nations who are members of the north Atlantic group Canada's obligations should be stated quite clearly. It was my understanding when the house approved Canada's signature to the North Atlantic treaty that we were obligated to fight if any of the countries who were signatory to that treaty was attacked. Article 5 of the treaty reads:
The parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them allin other words, an attack on one of the countries in Europe would be considered by Canada as an attack on Canada.
-and, consequently they agree that, if such an armed attack occurs, each of them, in exercise of the right of individual or collective self-defence recognized by article 51 of the charter of the United Nations, will assist the party or parties so attacked by taking forthwith, individually and in concert with the other parties, such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force-
Those are very important words.
-to restore and maintain the security of the north Atlantic area.
Then there is further reference to informing the security council. That appears to be a binding obligation on every nation a party to the treaty to supply a fighting force provided any one of the nations is attacked. Some doubt has been thrown on that by the statements of the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs this afternoon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Could the minister answer my second question? If such an attack took place in western Germany tonight would we be obligated to fight there in addition to our present obligation to fight in Korea?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I thought I had made that clear. But I take it that that would not interfere with any obligation we may have in Korea at this time. We would have two attacks to meet, one in Europe because of our membership in the Atlantic pact and one in Korea because of our membership in the United Nations.

When I was speaking earlier this afternoon I asked the minister if he would answer this question: With the world situation as it has been pictured this afternoon and our obligations under the United Nations charter and the Atlantic pact, there seems to be a very good possibility that we shall have to supply troops, other than the Korean brigade, at some future date. The Minister of National Defence has said that in case of hostilities the permanent force will have the role of training other forces. Therefore they will not be available to go out of the country. If we are engaged in Korea the Korean brigade will be occupied there. I ask the minister what plans the government has to provide the forces we would be called on to supply, having in mind the delay of about six to eight months that has been necessary to get the Korean brigade ready. If we have no trained forces we shall require a lapse of about six to eight months to prepare
Defence Appropriation Act them. Have we some plan to get around the delay of six to eight months, or do we plan on always taking that period of time to prepare forces if we are ever asked for them in the future under the Atlantic pact or by the United Nations Organization?
There is another question I asked and which I have not had answered. On June 26 last I asked the Minister of National Defence whether he did not consider that we required a division for the defence of Canada. At that time he said no, that he and his department considered that the brigade group we have at the present time was quite sufficient. Now it has become evident that we have never had a brigade group as such. We have three airborne battalions that have never worked together, have no headquarters and no signal section, and would require several weeks- the hon. member for Nanaimo estimates it would be closer to two months-before the brigade group could fight as a formation. Therefore since June 26 up to the present time we have not had the brigade group which the minister assured me that we had on that day in the house, because it has not been an effective fighting unit. I also want to ask him how long it will be before the brigade group is ready to fight as a unit in the defence of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Both questions have been asked before, and I believe both questions have been answered as fully as it is possible to answer them. However, I will make another effort. The time it will take to get a division ready depends on circumstances that I cannot anticipate at this moment, but that time will steadily decrease with the further recruitment and training of the armed forces of Canada, both active and reserve. The time it will take will depend on when we begin.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: When are you going to start? That is what I want to know.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We are not going to start to raise a division at the present time. That is not a part of our plan. I have said so to the hon. member and the committee generally, and have given the reasons why that is so. If circumstances change and it becomes a part of our plan to raise a division in peacetime, then that will obviously shorten the delay necessary to get that division into action as a fighting division in war. But if we do not decide to raise a division in peacetime then the delay involved- in raising it will depend upon when we begin, and what the degree of training is of the active and reserve forces at the time.
I should like to say a further word with respect to having a division in Canada. The hon. member made a serious suggestion and

Defence Appropriation Act I treated it seriously and with the benefit of the advice of the members of the general staff. I should like to add this point. If we are to have a division in being, then for it to be a division in being, ready to fight at the drop of a hat, it should be located for continuous training in one place. I think the hon. member will agree with that. That would mean having a force in peacetime of about 20,000, plus an administrative and training force of perhaps 10,000, plus wives and dependents and all the attendant services and amenities that go to make up a community. Therefore if we are going to keep this division together in Canada so that it is in training and ready to fight from day to day, I submit we would have a community of
30,000	plus, a very considerable operation.
That would require housing and services on a very large scale. I have seen communities in the United States where they have divisions, for instance, Fort Benning, and they are very large communities indeed. If we do not keep the division together in being and under training then it ceases to be a division that is ready to fight at the drop of a hat. As we envisage the defence needs of Canada they do not require the presence of a division in being in Canada at any one locality or at several localities. They require the elements in the brigade group in the state of training that they are today. In time the brigade group will receive training of the month or two months necessary to enable it to fight instantly as a unit. That is not considered to be necessary today as we think their time is being better occupied.
If elements in the division that the hon. member proposes are to be scattered about the country in brigades or battalions of infantry, regiments of artillery and the like, there is no very great advantage in having them called a division over the situation we have today. As I pointed out, we have in the active forces elements making up about three-quarters of those that would be required to form a division. That will be reduced when the force training for service under the United Nations is concentrated and moved out of Canada, if that is decided upon, as we expect it will be. But meanwhile recruiting will have gone on. Therefore I submit the hon. member's desire to have a division in being is partly met by the existing situation, and that will change and develop steadily. We do not mean to stand still. If the situation should develop in such a way that we find it both necessary and desirable to use our resources of men and money in some other way, then of course that change will be worked out.

With respect to the suggestion that we should have a division, I do not want to make comparisons with other countries, but I recall to the committee that the leader of the opposition said there were twelve divisions in western Europe, and I dare say hon. members know how many there are in each of the various countries of western Europe, including the United Kingdom. A division in being in peacetime in a country like Canada would be a very considerable undertaking. If we were to undertake that, it would constitute a very considerable advance. On the other hand we secure a very large part of the benefits of having a division in being from having active and reserve forces constituted as they are at present.
Just as a final word on this subject, I would like to ask hon. members what would have been the position if in 1946, when we were reorganizing the armed forces, we had adopted this suggestion.

I wonder if the minister would tell the committee what arrangements are being made for special officer training. During the last war, as many hon. members know, the largest officer training centre in Canada was located in the town of Brockville. That camp was to be declared surplus the latter part of this summer and handed over to the crown assets corporation, but only recently it was announced that the camp was to be taken off the surplus list. Naturally any community in which there was a camp during the war, which camp has been taken off the surplus

list, is anxious to know what is to become of it. In the case of Brockville, many of the buildings are in good condition; others are in pretty fair condition, while of course others, having been built for only ten years, have lived their lives. Of course we are anxious to see the camp reopened. It is interesting to recall that the training camp to which I am referring was commanded for over a year by a man of such distinction as the present Minister of Labour. I believe we would all like to know exactly what are the plans of the department with regard to the special training of officers.

speechtext:
I am sure hon. members are familiar with the plans for training officers in peacetime, under which we have arrangements for training university students for each of the three services. All twenty-seven universities are co-operating magnificently in this work. Under that arrangement the men do some extra work throughout their academic year and then put in full-time service for three or four months during the summer, so that at the end of their academic course they have a university degree and the equivalent of a year's practical training. This is working out admirably in all three services.
Then we have the Canadian service colleges at R.M.C. and Royal Roads where men are being trained for all three services. That is a four-year course, and if the men are in the technical branches they are sent at government expense to take their final year at a university. These two systems qualify men to exactly the same standards; they intermingle during the summer. There is also a third arrangement under which officers for the army are trained locally in command contingent corps, also to the same standards. These arrangements are very flexible, so that men can achieve the same standards in a number of different ways. Under one system or another we have over six thousand officers in training at the present time, so that to a very large degree we are meeting current needs in each locality and also, to a smaller degree, building up a pool of trained officers across 'the nation. In the event of an emergency this would enable us to meet the first shock and have time to accelerate training under arrangements such as those in effect during the second world war, at Brockville or other places that might be selected, where officers would receive accelerated courses lasting probably six months, and where they could develop just as speedily as possible. We also plan to have a great deal of on-the-job training for technical officers after they receive basic training.
Whether or not Brockville would be reopened for this purpose has not been decided, G9262-23
Defence Appropriation Act but pending further developments we are keeping hold of the camp there. The R.C.R. were at that camp until last year, and now they are at Petawawa. They had very good relations with the town of Brockville, and I think both were sorry when the unit had to leave.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am sure there is not a member of this house who is not fully cognizant of the fact that the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs are carrying heavy burdens of responsibility at this time. That is one reason why in contributions to the debates during this special session members of the official opposition have at all times stressed their desire to be constructive, co-operative and helpful. I urge upon the Minister of National Defence, who has taken the lead in rejecting a very useful suggestion for furthering that co-operation, that it is not too late to reconsider his stand in relation to that proposal. I am not going to labour the point, which has been thoroughly discussed, but I am going to ask the minister if he thinks that at this stage he is contributing very much by what appears to be a stubborn refusal to consider a proposal which has worked well in other fields and which it seems to me is capable of working efficiently and to the general advantage of parliament and the country in the field of national defence. It is paradoxical to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs sitting beside the Minister of National Defence while that minister categorically rejects the suggestion that a committee of this house be set up to deal with matters pertaining to national defence, since the Secretary of State for External Affairs is one minister who has contributed much to furthering the efficiency of one or more of the committees of the house. As you and I well know, Mr. Chairman, no standing committee of this house has worked better than the standing committee on external relations, and I think that is a perfect parallel.
Why it is that a principle can work so well in this house in the field of external relations, and build up within that sphere a spirit of co-operation among political parties, and yet, in spite of that fact some of the ministers deem it to be so unworthy even of experiment in the field of national defence? The answers that have been given to repeated requests for the establishment of such a committee in the interests of parliamentary efficiency in dealing with a national crisis have been weak. They have done no justice to the mental powers of those ministers who have put them forward. Even at this late period in the debate, Mr. Chairman, I would urge

Defence Appropriation Act the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Clax-ton) to give that subject renewed consideration. What advantage is it to Canada or to parliament for the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to throw out challenges and also crack the whip for the benefit of his followers as he did in the house one day last week when he said if we have been slow in rearming the country and preparing it for this crisis, then of course we should be voted out of office, and in the same breath say there is not going to be any committee, through which channel the members of this house could obtain the information they require to reach a decision as to whether the government has been measuring up to its responsibility in reference to the defence of the nation? That sort of attitude simply defeats any opportunity the house might have of addressing its intelligence to its responsibility in answering that important question.
I propose, sir, to be as direct and as brief as I can be in touching on two or three highlights in this question of our national defence position, and then to treat briefly two subjects that, so far as I know, have not been mentioned by any member in this discussion. In the first place, I wish we could obtain a common statement from the government ministers with reference to the extent of the emergency that exists. Listening to the Prime Minister when he spoke in the house last week it seemed to me, and I think to all members of the house, that the Prime Minister was seized with the extreme gravity of the situation. At times he described it in very serious terms. It seemed to me he was indicating an awareness of the existence of a critical emergency; but although I have been following the Minister of National Defence carefully, in his statements thus far I cannot detect any indication of a parallel attitude to that which I thought I found in the Prime Minister's statement. If I correctly understood the Prime Minister's position there is a very grave and critical emergency facing this country and the other free nations of the world. If I follow what the Minister of National Defence says, it seems as though there is plenty of time to experiment, that we may go this way or we may go that way, that we are keeping our planning very fluid so we can adjust ourselves to circumstances as they arise. Apparently there is nothing yet that calls for the government to grapple with an existing situation. For my part I should like to hear from the Minister of National Defence, since he has a very great responsibility now, as we all know, some indication of a sense of gripping urgency and critical emergency in the situation that confronts Canada.
Korea has at least nakedly exposed the danger of aggression. Aggressions were being

practised elsewhere. In all fairness and in all accuracy it cannot be said that the government did not have warning of the necessity for a measure of preparation for a situation of the kind that confronts us now.
It is crystal clear that there is, on the part of the members of this house, the utmost readiness to vote public money for the defence of Canada. There have been differences of view expressed in this debate as to the extent of commitments, and as to the particular direction in which Canadian assistance should be sent. At no particular time, or even in the present situation so far as I am aware, has any member of this house said that there should be any tying of the hands of the government in meeting the situation. If the government will only take us into its confidence, ask us for what is required by way of money to meet the needs of defence, there will be no haggling on the part of the members as long as the house is given the information, and as long as the house is satisfied the Canadian people are going to receive value for their money. In his war memoirs Mr. Churchill has said:
It is much better for parties or politicians to be turned out of office than to imperil the life of the nation. Moreover, there is no record in our history of any government asking parliament and the people for the necessary measures of defence and being refused.
Sir, that applies to the attitude of this house on this occasion.
I said, sir, that the Canadian people and, I hope, this house, wish to see value for our expenditures on national defence. Again Mr. Churchill says in his war memoirs:
Don't hamper departments acting in a time of crisis; give them the responsibility; but call them swiftly to account for any failure in thrift.
Applying that injunction from the great war leader, one is entitled to call this government swiftly to account for any failure in thrift. That, sir, is precisely what this house is trying to do at this time, and certainly what the members of the opposition are trying to do in the face of difficulties and obstacles put in their way because of the fact that we are denied, for various reasons, information that we say we are entitled to have.
Cannot the Minister of National Defence see that there is no party in this house that wants to be unfair in judging whatever preparations he can show have been made with these large expenditures of money, the hard-earned money of the Canadian taxpayers? We are palpably left in the dark. and, from past experience, unless we are given a great deal more information than has as yet been forthcoming, we can only conclude that that money has not been expended to the best advantage,

and that the Canadian people have not been given value for the expenditure of their money on national defence.
In measuring what the situation calls for and the need for forces in being, I wish the Minister of National Defence-I do not say this in any spirit of carping criticism-would be much clearer than he has been on this subject of commitments. This is no occasion for any play on words. Surely in a situation of this kind, where parliament is being called upon to vote vast sums of money, there is no time for playing upon words. What we want from the government are clear and understandable statements that admit of no misunderstanding or ambiguity. This afternoon the Minister of National Defence said we have no military commitments. Would it not have been much truer if the minister had said we have no military commitments apart from those clear commitments to which we have subscribed in the North Atlantic treaty? He was asked about commitments on April 3, 1950, when he returned from the meeting of the North Atlantic council and the subject of training in this country soldiers for the other North Atlantic nations arose. At page 1471 of Hansard the minister said:
We have our obligations under the treaty. The only additional obligation is the offer I have made, which is in course of being accepted, for the training of army personnel and aircrew. There are no other specific commitments.
Let us not split hairs about specific commitments. There are great and clear commitments in this pact to which Canada is a party; and unless these are commitments on Canada's part, we do not enjoy today the benefits we thought we enjoyed for the defence of Canada under this North Atlantic pact. We did not go into this simply because we thought we were giving something away. We entered into that pact because we thought that, by our becoming subscribers to that treaty, there was a great gain to be had for the defence of Canada. We should not wish to whittle down these commitments because, sooner than we care to think about it, we might wish to claim the benefit of the commitments on the part of other nations to that treaty.
I have spoken about the attitude of the house. In the absence of full information to the contrary, we can only conclude that the government has been slow and that its attitude has been marked by inertia. Again, Mr. Chairman, I quote from Mr. Churchill:
Virtuous motives, trammelled by inertia and timidity, are no match for armed and resolute wickedness.
We and the other free nations of the world are confronted today with armed and resolute wickedness. In that situation virtuous motives, 69262-23J
Defence Appropriation Act trammelled by inertia and timidity, are not enough; and we call upon the government to cast off those trammels of inertia and timidity.
Naturally we are not thinking simply in terms of the defence of Canada by Canada. We have to take account of all measures that we are entitled to look to for the defence of Canada; and from the discussions of the North Atlantic council and from statements that have since been made by responsible statesmen representing the free nations, it seemed quite clear that what the free nations are contemplating now is something of a functional collective preparation for the meeting of aggression. Collective preparation for collective self-defence seemed to be what we might expect following the statements issued after the last meeting of the North Atlantic council. I should therefore like to ask the Minister of National Defence if the particular measures that are being contemplated by the Canadian government-and I mean particular measures; I am not speaking in generalities -have been undertaken in consultation with the other nations of the North Atlantic pact, if the particular form of our defence preparations has been taken in consultation with the other nations who are members of that treaty arrangement.
I now mention a subject that I think is of direct concern to us. We are a long way from Korea, but the events there have made themselves felt in every part of Canada. How did it happen that the forces of aggression from north of the 38th parallel in Korea were able to burst their way over that parallel and flood southern Korea? How did it happen that there was here, apparently, a disastrous failure of intelligence? I do not know on whom the Canadian government was relying for intelligence in this situation. It may be that the Canadian government is not equipped to seek intelligence at these danger points in various places in the world. It may be that we must rely upon the intelligence facilities of the United States in certain areas and of the United Kingdom in other areas. But whatever the situation is, we have a direct concern in it because unquestionably there was a lamentable failure of intelligence in Korea, and we are bearing a share of the consequences.
We know that Mr. Dulles was there in Korea just a few days before the aggression burst over the boundary, and that he made an inspection, talked to some of the people there and apparently came away without any fear of imminent aggression. Perhaps others were still thinking of the trumpeting Russia made on her withdrawal from Korea, strangely enough on Christmas day, 1948. I was looking over some press clippings

Defence Appropriation Act I had on this subject and, in the light of later events, I was amazed to find that as far back as May 10 not some irresponsible person but a member of the government of the republic of South Korea made a statement warning the nations of the world that aggression was about to burst over the border. This is a Canadian Press dispatch coming from Seoul, Korea, dated May 10. It is brief, and it reads as follows:
The independent republic of South Korea is threatened with invasion by the communist forces of North Korea, defence minister Sihn Sung Mo of the southern republic warned today.
Sihn today said intelligence reports indicate that forces of the north are moving toward the 38th parallel. He gave a breakdown of forces available to communist Korea.
The north Korean army totals 183,000 trained men, he reported. It has 173 planes, 173 tanks and 32 naval vessels. In addition there are 9,000 trained guerrillas plus communist constabulary and youth corps units. These forces, Sihn added, include about 25,000 north Koreans who fought with the Chinese communists and now have returned home to aid their own country's red forces.
That was a warning coming on May 10 last from the minister of defence of the republic of South Korea, six weeks in advance of the attack. That timely warning apparently fell on deaf ears. The nations of the free world, including our own nation, have since been feeling the disastrous effects of the aggression that has taken place; and those disastrous effects were attributable at least in part to the fact that either there was a deplorable lack of intelligence or those who were receiving intelligence reports were not acting upon them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when
speaking last week on the subject now before the house, the present crisis, I went to some length to point out that we cannot and dare not rely on military action alone. I am rather disturbed at the extent to which reference to other weapons that could be used against communism has been omitted in this debate. The speaker who has just taken his seat referred to some of the weapons against communism which the free nations have at their disposal, but he too failed to refer to the one great factor which today makes communism desirable to vast masses of people in Asia. I refer to the fact that the western world in the past has failed to show those people that democracy as we know it in the west can serve them for their own needs and not for the purpose of satisfying western greed and western profit.
I should like to speak for a few moments on the military side of this matter because I realize, as does every hon. member, that in the world as it is constituted today and when we are faced with such danger as we are faced with today there must be adequate military preparations.
As I said last week, force must be used to meet aggression when force is the weapon the aggressor chooses to use, as is the case in Korea. If one is to survive, force must be met with still greater force. Because of that I have no choice, as other hon. members have no choice, but to support the government in the measures now before us for the purpose of strengthening our military forces. I support those measures, yet at the same time I believe they are but half


measures, merely stopgaps. In themselves they cannot possibly help us win the long fight against communism that lies ahead.
Because of the importance of military preparedness I find that I must ally myself with those who have been critical of the government's lack of preparedness as was shown to us when the Korean situation broke. When the security council issued its appeal for military support I was surprised to learn that we were able to give such little support. When the Prime Minister issued his statement in June he assured us that if more help were needed by the United Nations than the ships the government had already undertaken to send, parliament would be called to approve the sending of such forces. I never dreamed for a moment that parliament would have to be called together to authorize the government to enlist and raise the forces that would be sent to Korea. I took it for granted that, with the expenditures on national defence of somewhere near a billion and a half since the last war, we were much better prepared at the present time than the facts reveal. Members of the house, whose military records and experience lend some weight to the statements they make, have charged that at the time of the outbreak in Korea the government did not have any troops sufficiently trained or organized to go into immediate action either to defend Canada against attack or to fulfil our obligations to the United Nations or to our allies under the North Atlantic pact.
I have heard no denial of that charge on the part of the minister or the government. I have heard a great many excuses given by the minister, but I submit that the taxpayers of Canada, and certainly if not the taxpayers their elected representatives in this house, are entitled to know with some degree of clarity what we have by way of military forces and what we have accomplished in military preparation for the billion and a half dollars voted by parliament in the last few years. In my opinion, if the minister thinks he cannot, because of security reasons, give in open session the kind of information that opposition members are asking for, then I for one agree with the leader of the opposition who appealed for a secret session of the house. We found secret sessions helpful during the last war. I am not sure that we were given much information in the secret sessions which I had the privilege of attending that could not have been given in open session of the house, but I do know that we were given much more detailed information than we were able to secure in open sessions.
So far as I know, national security did not suffer by reason of those secret sessions.

What is true is that opposition members, and I suspect many government members, felt that they were being taken into the government's confidence with some degree of dignity and with some regard for the responsibility of elected representatives to their constituents. The cabinet of that day did not assume to itself the attributes of omniscience and omnipotence that the present cabinet assumes in its dealings with the house. They did not assume that they were the only group in the house with all the knowledge obtainable on any given subject. Nor did they assume that degree of all-powerfulness that the present government appears to be assuming.
I submit that if the government cannot answer in. open session the very relevant and pointed questions asked by opposition members, then by all means they should be answered in a secret session of the house while we are here at this time. Members of the house are entitled to that information. Otherwise they become nothing more than mere rubber stamps for cabinet decisions. Again let me say, Mr. Chairman, that it is not in the best interests of good government that the Canadian people should conclude that the government has anything to hide from parliament or the public regarding its expenditures on national defence. Certainly that is the impression which is going abroad across the country as a result of the opposition of the Minister of National Defence and the other cabinet ministers to the request of opposition members for a parliamentary committee or a secret session of parliament where more information can be given and where there is an opportunity to learn just what the government is doing with the money we vote.
The very nature of the Department of National Defence with its extensive ramifications, as pointed out by the Minister of National Defence yesterday, is only a reason for the closest possible scrutiny by parliament of expenditures by that department. There is abroad the impression that the Department of National Defence is the one government department in which money is wasted in huge amounts. It is probably inevitable that there should be waste in war expenditures of any kind. It is pretty generally agreed throughout the country that during the last war, although no public scandal was uncovered, literally millions of dollars were squandered in war expenditures. That merely points up the necessity at this time of parliament being afforded every possible opportunity to cooperate with the government in an effort to get good value for the moneys spent.
On the question of the time lag between the date when the security council called
Defence Appropriation Act for assistance and the time when the government finally made up its mind to raise ground forces for Korea, I can only say that as yet no sound reason has been given to parliament for the delay. It is true that the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave us certain reasons, but, with all the regard I have for him, I must say that those reasons were not very convincing. I even wondered whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs was himself convinced of their soundness. It would seem to me the government were more concerned with the possible political repercussions of any speedy action that might be taken at that point than with the exigencies of the situation. That could be; and I believe this house is entitled to more information than we have yet received.
Now I want to turn for a few moments from the military aspect to the phase emphasized by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he said we cannot hope to win in this crisis by military power alone. In recent years vast numbers of people in all parts of the world have come to embrace communism because it gives them some hope of attaining one of the freedoms mankind has sought throughout its entire history; that is, freedom from hunger. Because communism has held out to the world that promise of freedom from hunger it has appealed to hungry millions the world over. It was a similar promise by fascists and nazis during the thirties that won for them the support of millions of people in central Europe. To men and women iri any country, at any time, who have to go literally half-starved and watch their children suffer hunger, freedom from hunger becomes of paramount importance. Freedom of parliament, freedom of the press, freedom of assembly, freedom of enterprise and even freedom of religion all take second place to freedom from hunger, in the minds of a half-starved people. It is because communism has always held out and still holds out the promise of freedom from hunger- which, incidentally, imperialist capitalism has failed to assuage in Asia during the past hundred years-that millions of people in Asia are turning not to democracy but to communism. We have only to read the story of rubber or oil or any of our great industrial empires that have been built upon the oppression of eastern peoples and the exploitation of their natural resources to see why it should be so comparatively easy today for Russia to persuade the people of the east that she is their liberator, that western nations have been and still are their oppressors. What the peoples of the east want today is not so much liberation from their own despots as liberation from western oppression and exploitation. Our problem, as western democracies

Defence Appropriation Act anxious to preserve whatever degree of democracy we have attained, is to offset in the east in the shortest possible time the injustices we have been inflicting upon these people for the last hundred years. We shall not have a hundred years in which to do that. We shall not have fifty years. We shall be lucky if we have ten years in which to put our own houses in order and in which to convince the peoples of the east that democracy as we know it can be made to function in their day-to-day lives. Just so long as the economic benefits of democracy accrue to a comparatively small, privileged group, while millions abroad and hundreds of thousands in our own country devote all their energies to eking out a bare existence, all our high-sounding phrases about democratic freedom will have little meaning, and little effect against communism.
I believe communism is a blind alley up which a great section of mankind is stumbling today in its drive toward a better way of life, a drive which constitutes a sort of divine spark in human nature. Unless mankind annihilates itself in an atomic war-and I have far too much confidence in homo sapiens to believe that homo is such a sap as to do any such thing-I believe mankind eventually will find its way back to a through thoroughfare which will lead it closer to its eternal goal.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I must say that even if it were possible for us to defeat Russia in an atomic war or any other kind of war as decisively as we defeated Germany and Italy in the last war, we would only scotch the snake and not kill it. As the leader of our group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, said a few days ago, communism is an idea; and you cannot kill an idea with bullets. Somehow we must show those who are being attracted to communism that our way of life can bring them more happiness without depriving them of the freedoms they wish, and without requiring the sacrifice of any material benefit which communism may be able to offer. This government can give leadership to the world at the forthcoming assembly of the United Nations by showing its readiness to contribute, through the appropriate committees and councils of that organization, to the abolition of poverty and starvation through the introduction of measures which will assist undeveloped countries of the world to develop their own resources for their own use. What is needed at home to win the battle against communism, and to properly arm us in this conflict, is for the government to bring down some legislation that will effectively cope with the spiral of rising prices that confronts us today;


legislation that will prevent undue profiteering out of the $800 million that we are being asked to vote in this session.
If you think that matter is not important, you have only to glance over today's newspapers. I have a series of clippings from the Toronto Globe and Mail which give a fairly good picture of our situation today. Concerning the international situation there is this headline blazing across the front page: "United Nations flank crushed." On the second page there is an article concerned with the fact that a Red bomber was shot down yesterday while attacking United Nations forces. In another article in the same paper we read of the steps Red China is taking in order to influence and secure the support of the people of Tibet. Still further we hear that the people of New York are taking the present situation so seriously that they are restricting the use of the siren in New York to air raid signals only. That is the world as it is pictured in one issue of one paper.
Looking at the economic situation, here is a heading which tells us, "Abbott says arms bill is to hit living standards." In another article we find that the veterans are asking that the pension act be revised to cover the high cost of living. A further article in the same paper indicates that the united automobile workers are demanding United States wage rates. With prices rising, workers are beginning to grow restless and demand adequate salaries and wages. Still another heading says, "Railway running trades ask thirty per cent increase; deal with C.P.R. first." This is an indication of the ferment in which we find ourselves today, and shows the necessity for passing some legislation at this session which will curb that economic situation.
Turning to another phase of the same problem, we read that a trade union conference in Great Britain representing some 8 million trade unionists applauded Prime Minister Attlee who came into the congress asking the trade unionists to accept sacrifices in the interest of security. He was acclaimed as if he had brought a bigger pay packet to every man and woman in Britain. Why? I believe the answer is given in a short paragraph in the same article which reads:
The Prime Minister promised that the government would do its utmost to see that the sacrifices made for the nation's safety were fairly borne.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the people of Canada are asking that, if they are called upon to make sacrifices, whether it is the sacrifice of their sons or a reduction in their living standards, those sacrifices be borne fairly by all the Canadian people. They do not want to see once more sacrifices made by

large sections of the Canadian people, while a comparative few become millionaires as a result of war profiteering. The Canadian people do not want to again be called upon to make sacrifices under those circumstances. They will rally to the call of the government in this crisis as they rallied in the forties. But to get their support we in this parliament must give them some assurance that steps will be taken to curb the rising cost of living and to prevent profiteering.
