speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is another matter I should like to bring before this committee which has to do with the defence of Canada. It is a matter that has not been brought up by any of the speakers in the debate thus far. I refer to civil defence. I bring this matter before the committee not with any idea of causing alarm to the Canadian people, but conditions in warfare have changed. They have changed so greatly that now the civilian population might be considered to be in the front lines. In England in the last war during the intensive bombing, before the army ever saw any action, the civilian population suffered greatly. In fact, for some time in England it was said by way of a joke, "Join the army and be safe." The army got into action later and suffered severe casualties, but the civilian population suffered tremendous casualties.
For the past two or three days we have heard speeches about the defence of Canada. Mention has been made of battalions, brigades, divisions, aircraft; and many members are greatly concerned with the defence of Canada, and rightly so. But no nation is properly protected unless some recognition is taken of the civilian population. This morning in the C.B.C. news at eight o'clock I heard that the mayor of Windsor was very much concerned: over the safety of that large industrial city. Later in the morning papers I found two references indicating 'that people were concerned about civil defence. One item dealt with York township, north of Toronto, and the headline in the Globe and Mail states, "York spends $15 on atom defence." This is not a joke, and when I read the article you will see how serious it is. These men are looking for some direction from the government. The article reads:
York township council turned its attention yesterday to the defence of township citizens in the event of an atom bomb raid in this area. Councillors agreed to order twelve copies at $1.25 each of the United States atomic energy commission's new pamphlet The Effects of Atomic Weapons. Distribution will be to councillors, and the police, health and fire departments.
In the same paper, with the headline "Chief asks part in civil defence", is a dispatch from
69262-2i
Defence Appropriation Act the Canadian Press dated September 5. It reads:
Fire Chief Robert C. McRonald, of London, Ontario, today called for integration of the Dominion Association of Fire Marshals in Canada's civil defence scheme.
In his presidential address he said:
A body of men such as ours, responsible for protection of life and property in peace, is most certainly a tailor-made set-up in a national emergency.
The report continues:
Stressing the importance of the municipal fire authority in Canada's civil defence program, he said an alliance between the association and Ottawa's defence scheme "would make for a strong and compact organization; it would be ready for protection and defence at a moment's notice."
If such an alliance were formed, it would be imperative that the administrator of national defence keep the association posted on all latest developments concerning atomic, biological and chemical warfare.
Within security regulations, this data would be disseminated to points "deemed vulnerable to attack," he said.
I remember that last year a question was asked of the minister concerning what preparations had been made and what had been done toward training the civilian population of Canada in this matter. If I remember correctly, he intimated that if the people were organized now, and if some attempt were made at training the people, they would lose their enthusiasm, that the matter would wear out, and that they would come to disregard preparations.
I think this matter is altogether too serious for that. If this world condition has gone so. far that it is necessary to debate in the House of Commons the question of the defence of Canada and military preparations, I think this matter is of equal importance and that the civilian population should have some defence.
This country might occupy the same position as England occupied in the last war, or Belgium or Poland. The civilian population might suffer and the army, being occupied elsewhere, could not carry out this work. In fact, if the army were occupied in repelling an invader, their field ambulances, their medical staff and their field hospitals would be too much occupied to begin to attend to the civilian population. More than that, it would be difficult to spread this work over the whole of Canada in areas which might be subjected to bombing or in the event of widespread bombing of industrial areas.
I wish to say again that I bring this matter up for consideration not with any intention of alarming the population of this country. It is, however, an extremely important matter

Defence Appropriation Act at the present time. I am aware that the government has appointed General Worthington, an outstanding soldier, to do some work in this connection but with regard to this work I find that at the present time our preparations are vague. Certainly we have heard from three municipalities today, both by radio and by the press, that they are asking for some direction and that something be done about this matter. This is a matter that is of interest to every Canadian. If we send our army into action in the defence of Canada, if we have no preparations made for modern warfare, and if the civilian population suffers, then our defence plans are far from being complete. One is almost as important as the other.
I should like to give a short review of what might happen if this country were invaded. There are three possible dangers from warfare by air. One comes immediately to our minds-and it was mentioned by the last speaker-namely the question of bombing. Bombing might be by use of the explosive bomb, which by its explosive power destroys property; that is a tremendous agent in war. The other form of bombing might be by the use of the atomic bomb. Every member of this committee is aware of what happened in London in the last war with regard to explosive bombing, so tonight I am going to say a few words about the question of the atomic bomb.
We have had two examples of the effect of atomic bomb warfare on a civilian population, one in Hiroshima and the other in Nagasaki. There are certain lessons to be learned from what happened there. These lessons concern the defence of the civilian population. Not only was there a large area destroyed by the explosive force of the atomic bomb, but the people at the outer perimeter of the area that was bombed suffered terribly from burns and from the effects of rays released by the explosion of the atomic bomb. The people at these outer perimeters who escaped burning began to suffer weeks and months later from vague and unusual blood diseases in the forms of anaemia and leukemia. In any preparations made for the future we must therefore consider these two types of bombs.
The question of the explosive bomb, which by its very destructive power causes damage to property and loss of human life, would give the authorities in any municipality a tremendous question to deal with. But the picture with regard to the atomic bomb is entirely different. We would have to make preparation of another type to deal with such a condition. Medical men will find it difficult to deal with

some of the results which last for a long time after the actual explosion of the bomb has taken place.
There is another matter which might enter into our consideration-and I refer to aerial warfare-and it is the question of germ or bacterial warfare. This might take several courses. We have heard a great deal about it, and it is not a matter for light consideration.' In the event that the enemy used germ or bacterial warfare, it is apparent that he would try to infect our civilian population and cripple our industrial life by making ill the workers and labourers in the factories. Or it might be some form of germ warfare that would interfere with our food supplies, our water supplies or something of that nature. But one thing stands out clearly with regard to germ warfare. An attempt would be made to infect our civilian population with some organism which would be friendly to the enemy but which would cripple our people for the time being at least. It would be easy for an enemy to infect the population of this country, and at the same time it would put many of our factories out of business if our workers in those factories were infected with some of the diseases that could be used. I am not going to enter into the question of certain germs which could be used, but this is a matter for consideration.
Gas warfare is quite a possibility. In concentrated areas where a large population exists, it would be possible to use gas warfare in Canada, employing gases of certain types. That would mean that the civilian population would have to have some instruction in gas warfare; and certainly they would need something to help them out in the way of gas masks, training in resuscitation and in methods of helping people who had become casualties owing to gas.
I have mentioned three things that could happen in aerial warfare or invasion, namely the use of gases, the use of germ warfare, the use of the explosive bomb and the use of the atomic bomb. We would have to have certain defences against such a thing, if it ever happened in this country. Defence measures would certainly lead to an enlargement of all the facilities we have for treating casualties. Our hospitals at the present time are jammed to the doors. There would be no hope of those hospitals or the medical staffs in them taking care of an area where there was a concentrated attack by gas or bomb, so that some other arrangements would have to be made.
In the first place I think the most important of all would be instruction to the people cf Canada. The people who are at the head cf

the municipalities-the mayors-are aware that something may happen, and they are looking to the government for help and instruction. We would need to get busy at once and train a large personnel in first aid and in the treatment of people who had suffered from burns, or the various types of casualties which may occur in the new type of warfare.
It takes a long time to train personnel in this work. It is all very well to say that if the occasion arises we are going to do this or that; but you cannot train first-aid help in a short time. If we are going to have this country fully prepared for the care of our civilian population we should get busy at once and train personnel and make arrangements for the care of casualties. It is necessary then that we think of some form of hospital care at first, so that in every municipality arrangements would be made for some place other than hospitals to take care of casualties-because the hospitals are full.
Some plans should be made for the use of church basements, or some place where there would be some form of protection where the work of first aid could be carried out-because as I said before, we have to go somewhere other than hospitals. The arrangements that could be made in each municipality would be directed by the municipal councils, so long as personnel were trained in each municipality and so long as some place were provided to which these casualties could be taken.
That brings me to the question of the care of casualties. One of the first thoughts to come to my mind is that of the building up of an adequate blood bank. In the last war there was some measure of preparation but, so far as the blood banks were concerned, they were for the use of the soldiers overseas, although they were used partially also for the use of our own population.
This work could again be started, and something done to build up the blood banks, which are so important in the treatment of casualties, and particularly the type of casualties one would get in a war where there would be injuries from bombing. When people are afflicted through bombing the first thing to do is to carry out a blood transfusion, before any attempt at surgery is made.
Then there should be plans made for the evacuation of large centres, so that the people could be sent somewhere. It would be all very well, for instance, to say that the city of Ottawa was to be evacuated: where would it be evacuated to? The people could not be sent to the surrounding towns, because 69262-241
Defence Appropriation Act they suffer from a housing shortage, and there would be no place for the extra population.
Something must be done. In the event of actual bombing there is the need of known places of shelter to which people could be taken so that they might be safe from the bombs. The atomic bomb makes necessary some changes in the type of shelter required. Already the United States government has put out pamphlets and given some instruction to their people about what should be done. In one of the papers I saw some excellent diagrams in which direction was given as to how to build a bomb shelter, and particularly a bomb shelter that would be effective against an atomic bomb.
It is important also, so far as the government is concerned, that there should be selected areas or depots for the storage of food, and especially for the storage of drugs and surgical supplies. There should be central depots from which such supplies could be drawn, and such depots would have to be placed in every area so that every town or city in the country would have some place from which they could draw emergency supplies.
I have mentioned the question of the contamination of food supplies through germ warfare. It is most important that the water supply be protected, and that there be close co-operation between the people and the bacteriological laboratories. The same co-operation would be required if an attempt were made by an enemy to contaminate the milk or water supplies, or to plant diseases in the animals of this country. Veterinary and medical organizations should be alerted to the possible danger of such a thing happening. This is a very important matter, just as important as any plan we may make for the future regarding the repelling of any force invading our country.
The fire chief of London quite properly, at the convention in Victoria, brought the matter of defence before that convention. No doubt he was concerned about fire protection, and that there might be danger from fifth columnists who would try to interfere with our large factories. Or, as was found in England in the last war, there might be some danger of fire from bombs. The civilian population should be organized to take part. That is one branch of civil defence that would not take too long to organize, and I appeal to the government that some arrangements be made for the defence of the population against the gas and bomb warfare to which I have referred. Such excellent organizations as the Red Cross and the St. John Ambulance

Defence Appropriation Act Association would need some time to train personnel, to prepare supplies and, in general, to prepare to combat such a condition if it should arise through an invasion of this country.
Remember, it is just as important that the civilian population and those people who produce foods and who work in our industries be protected as it is to protect the army in the field. Conditions of warfare have changed, and this has become a vitally important subject.
I am not going to speak at length on this matter, but in view of what I read this morning, that these municipal authorities are asking for help, and the further fact that nothing is being done about it at the present time, I felt I should speak. There may be some plan and some organization; but even if such a plan could be put into operation, there would still be some problems.
The minister spoke this morning about the length of time it takes to train a body of troops. It would take a great deal longer time to train a highly efficient personnel who would deal with matters of this kind. The minister suggested that there might be some possibility of their becoming careless about their work if they were in training for a long time and nothing happened. I do not think the Canadian people would lose their enthusiasm, if they saw the necessity.
Let us remember this, that the longer the training went on the more efficient would the personnel become. It would not be a matter of simply giving a first aid course, but instruction which would lead1 to handling casualties efficiently.
I leave this matter with the government and appeal to every member of the house by saying that this matter is just as important as the other matters we have been discussing. Let us hope that no use need ever be made of the trained personnel or of the defence measures I have mentioned. If any use were made of it, it would not be an expensive arm of the service and the training received by these people would be useful all their lives. Nothing would be lost. But there should be some direction from the government, something more than vague intimations once in a while that they are doing something about it.
This morning the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to the accident at Peta-wawa. I do not intend to discuss a matter under investigation by the authorities, but I do suggest that some training along industrial accident prevention lines should be given these men. Sometimes familiarity breeds contempt and people who are handling explosives become careless. I remember quite well the


trench mortars of the first war. Nobody knew whether they were going to start or where they would go. I do not blame anyone in this matter but I do think the personnel should be instructed that they are dealing with dangerous materials.
Two other cases have occurred not far from the city of Ottawa. An Ottawa high school student was blinded by a grenade at Hogs-back. I do not know how the grenade got there, and I do not think anyone knows, but in some way it got out of army stores. The court has held that the army is not responsible, yet the fact remains that this boy is blinded for life. A short time ago two children received eye injuries and serious burns close to Petawawa camp. I do not know how it happened, but the fact remains that the two children were seriously hurt.
A closer check should be kept on army stores. When you consider the boy blinded at Ottawa, the two little children who received eye injuries and burns at Petawawa and the four soldiers who were killed and the others who were injured at Petawawa camp you have a rather high total of casualties for peacetime. There were a number of casualties following the war owing to the fact that the boys brought home different weapons, and such casualties are still occurring.
Accidents will occur when you are dealing with weapons of this type, but I repeat that a closer check should be made of the men handling these dangerous things. The hon. member for Cape Breton South brought out the point this morning that only skilled instructors or men who realize what they are handling should have to do with these weapons. That is all I am going to say on the matter.	\
We have had a debate on the possibilities of the invasion of Canada and the defensive measures we are taking, and I think we should also seriously consider what should be done for the civilian population. I hope the need for what I have suggested will never occur; I hope that this organization will never have to go into action, but we should be prepared for what might happen to our civilian population.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Everyone appreciates the
interest shown by the hon. member for Lanark in health and welfare matters. There are one or two brief comments I should like to make. Lest there be an impression that there have been a large number of civilian losses due to explosives used by the armed forces, may I state to the committee that since 1939 there have been just twenty such incidents. There were four cases in which the crown was found to be negligent and in those cases payment

was made. There were a number of other cases where there was no legal responsibility but there might be moral responsibility and applications were submitted for ex gratia payments, which were made. That is a good record considering the fact that we .had thousands of establishments at which high explosives were used.
The hon. member has suggested that during exercises with live ammunition there should be present personnel trained along the lines of those engaged in industrial accident prevention work. The instructions are that on all such occasions there is to be a safety officer with each group of men. My experience is that this is done. I have no reason to believe that such officer was not present when the regrettable accident occurred at Petawawa. Perhaps the hon. member was not in the house today when I gave an indication of the cause of that accident in so far as it has been reported to me.
Civil defence of course is an important question. Recently we had a conference with the provinces which resulted in an understanding of lines of responsibility and action. The results of that conference were communicated to the provinces and are under consideration, r do not want to go into them because the conference was confidential, but I would point out that while the federal government accepts responsibility for leadership in this field, the actual working forces for civil defence must, of necessity, be handled by local authorities.
I do not suggest for a second that the responsibility is entirely local, but I do suggest that, the agencies for carrying out that responsibility, such as police, firemen and so on, must be related to the ordinary civil life of the community. In our experience in dealing with the Fraser river and the Manitoba floods and the Rimouski and Cabano fires it was found that the federal authorities, acting through the military arm, could best carry out their functions by backing up and supporting the civil authorities in their respective field.
However, civil defence in time of war is another problem. The character of the possible disaster is quite different. The federal government must accept and does accept responsibility for planning the organization at the higher level, but the arrangements that are being worked out with the provinces indicate that they will have their role and deal with the municipalities in their several aspects. We believe that is a very important principle to be worked out at this stage. Later it may be necessary to change that relationship but at the present stage the best
Defence Appropriation Act way in which the federal government can deal with municipalities, which must be the local agencies for dealing with civil defence, is through and with the provinces. That has been the basis on which we have discussed the matter with the provinces, and we have not yet had a full expression of their views.
Something was said about three forms of warfare-A, B, and C. With respect to biological and chemical warfare, Canada has probably done as much work as any country on defence against this kind of warfare. Our defence research board is keeping well abreast, and in fact ahead, of most developments in that field. With regard to atomic warfare, the hon. member has no doubt seen various reports on this subject, and I can also assure him that, through our experience gained from the developments we are conducting on the civil side of Chalk River, we are well up with developments from the defence point of view. All these are being taken into account. I can assure the hon. member that his views will be given full consideration and effect. It will be a matter of weeks, if not of days, before we receive the views of the provinces on our discussions. Those will be communicated by them to the municipalities, and I am sure will produce results along the line he wants.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise tonight to speak in this defence debate with a deep sense of frustration. I think I have been here almost continuously during the discussion of
386	HOUSE OF
Defence Appropriation Act defence matters in the debate on the speech from the throne and on the present resolution. It has been a confused and diffused debate which is not producing very much specific information. The minister has not come to grips with the questions in the minds of the members and the people of the country. The way in which the debate has proceeded, and how little it has produced in answers to questions which people want answered, are the best indication of the good sense of a committee on defence. I thought the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South this morning was a model of good sense in that regard. He spoke of the futility of a debate of this kind so far as obtaining any real information about defence matters is concerned.
What are the main questions in the minds of the people of Canada relating to defence? The first one undoubtedly is why were there not fighting forces available, forces in being ready to fight, after some five years had elapsed and one and a half billion dollars had been spent on them from the end of the last war to the present time? That question is still unanswered. The minister has not given us any definite information as to where the money has gone and on what it has been spent.
Then there is another question in people's minds. How are the present large sums that are being asked for going to result in definite defences for this country? What is going to be the effect of them? What are we actually going to get so far as people are concerned who can fight and who will be ready to fight in the defence of Canada? I think the people of Canada are primarily interested in their own defence. After that they are interested in answering the call of the United Nations, living up to our agreements under the Atlantic pact, and so on. They want to live up to all commitments we have made, either specific or general, but the first thing they want to be assured about in their own minds is whether we have in Canada something with which to defend the country.
Their confidence, if they had any, that such was the case has been very rudely shaken during the last month and a half. I think it is now the first duty of the government to tell the country definitely and specifically what forces are in being and what forces will be in being for the next six months or a year, at which time it is hoped, according to the general information we have been given, that the defences of Canada will be in a reasonably prepared state. Instead of doing that, the minister continues with the theme of the well-known Mr. Coue, every day in every way we are getting better and better. Everything he says is in that vein. That
[Mr. Harkness.l

sort of course has worn thin. We do not want to hear anything more along that line. We have heard too much of it already, particularly with the lack of existing fighting forces to back up such words.
The minister said today that we could not have a division in Canada, and I think he added at the present time. He gave two reasons for that. He said first of all that it was not necessary at the present time, and second, that we could not afford it. So far as necessity is concerned, I think during the course of the day he went as far as to say that he would be very happy to have a division if it could be done within practical bounds. He has never said that it was necessary, but nevertheless he said he would be very glad to have it. My contention is that it is necessary. With the present condition of the world I think that a division of troops- and I mean regular troops who are in a position to fight if required-is necessary for the defence of Canada. Certainly if we are going to be able to meet any of our commitments, specific or general-I do not care what you call them because there is no use arguing over the terms of the commitments-we need a division. We know from what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that we have some commitments already. In order to meet any of those it is quite apparent that we must have larger armed forces, ready to fight, than we have at the present time; and I am sure nearly everyone in this country is convinced that we need more than we have now in order to look after the defence of this country alone.
Now I come to the second of the minister's contentions, that we cannot afford it; that it would be too expensive; that it would require twenty thousand men, with a further ten thousand to look after them. I do not know where the figure of twenty thousand came from. Unless I am very much mistaken the number of men in a division is much closer to fifteen thousand than twenty thousand. As far as the extra ten thousand to look after them is concerned, that has been one of the troubles of our defence set-up for many years past. For several years we have had large headquarters and administrative staffs which could have looked after very much greater numbers of people than we have had. So I doubt very much whether anything like the number of people mentioned by the minister would be required. Of course he exploded that idea himself by going on to say that already we are fairly well on the way to having a division, taking the airborne brigade, the special brigade and certain other units which are in being. The only reason we could not have a division in being in this country without expending an additional cent is that we are spending far too much on

needlessly large headquarters and administrative staffs. Go into national defence headquarters here in Ottawa, or command or area headquarters anywhere in the country; you wonder what all the people are doing. We are top-heavy in that regard; I do not think there is any doubt about that. I think there is no question but that by' cutting down our whole headquarters and administrative set-up, with the same amount of money or perhaps even less we could have a division in being, and could have had that division when this Korean trouble started. It is not a question of the total expenditure; it is a question of properly spending the money that has been voted.
In that connection it might be instructive to take a brief look at the fighting units that were in existence in 1938 and 1939, before the last war. People look back at that period and say in an offhand way, "Oh, we had nothing then. We are tremendously better off now than we were at that time." As a matter of fact, as far as fighting units are concerned, exactly the same units were in existence then that we have now. There are one or two more now; that is all. We had the three infantry battalions; we had the two cavalry regiments, as they were then; we had one artillery regiment, and some engineers and so on. Basically, however, the units in the regular army, the people who really go out and fight, were the same as they are now. It is true that we did not have nearly as many men in them as we have at the present time; but even at that, as far as I know we are only up to strength in one unit, unless conditions have changed within the last two months. When we consider the amount of money being spent on defence in 1938 and 1939 and the number enrolled in the regular forces at that time and compare it with the number in the regular forces now and the money being spent, it is simply amazing to realize that we have no more fighting units than we had then, no more units trained to go out with bayonets and do some hard work on the enemy if one should come in sight. We have more people in those units, that is all; and still they are not up to strength.
Several times during the past two or three days we have heard the minister say how much the reserve army has increased in strength in the last three years, that the percentage is up so much, and so on. I know something about a fair number of reserve units in my own province, and in my opinion those units are not in as good shape to mobilize at the present time as they were in 1939. In fact most of the units out there with which I am acquainted are not as well trained as they were then; they are not as well prepared to form the nucleus of a regiment or
Defence Appropriation Act battalion or whatever it may be. I am not blaming this entirely on the defence department. The reconstitution of those units following the war was bound to take some time and to be a difficult matter. The same thing occurred after the first world war; it took some years to get the reserve units reorganized and working. However, I do blame the government for not taking more energetic measures to get men into those units. The only thing that will make them successful and efficient is a proper number of men, with the necessary officers and N.C.O.'s to train them; and that is just what we have not had. I blame the government severely for not taking more energetic measures to get these units in better shape as far as personnel is concerned; and there has been no indication in what has been said during the past two days that any great change is to be made in that regard. All the minister has said is that they are going to expand the reserve units. How are they going to expand them? What specific plans have they to increase the number of men in those units? What definitely are they going to do to increase the personnel? As a matter of fact I think one of the difficulties in some places, at any rate, is that there are too many units, as I pointed out two or three years ago. Some places have been simply loaded down with units, and have so many it is not possible for any of them to get sufficient men because there just are not enough men available in the right age brackets and of the right type. I think perhaps some progress might be made in certain places by reducing the number of units, combining them or what you will, so the men actually available for the reserve army can be used more efficiently.
We have here, Mr. Chairman, essentially three matters to consider. The first is the regular force, and what expansion is to take place there. The second is the reserve force, about which I have just been talking. The third is the matter of civil defence, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Lanark. Last year and again this year we have followed the procedure of asking question after question each time extracting some little morsel of information from the minister with great difficulty. I suggest that we get away from that procedure and that the minister, perhaps while the budget debate is going on, get to work and1 put down in definite form all the information he feels he can give us, first under the heading of the regular force including the navy, army and air force, then the reserve force, and then civil defence. If he would come in here with a reasonably concise statement containing all the information he feels he can possibly give us in connection with these matters, in a well organized form,

Defence Appropriation Act I think it would considerably expedite the discussion of this whole matter. As it is all we are doing is drawing out a little information a morsel at a time. It is not getting us very far.
I should like to say a few words about the regular forces. It has developed, and it was apparent a year ago, that the navy is the only force which had units in being and ready to fight. Three destroyers were sent immediately to Korea, and other naval units are in home waters or on training cruises. It was the only service that had anything ready to go, and for that I commend the navy. I am glad there was one service that had some fighting units ready to fight. I trust the new ships which are now under construction, and which the minister says we shall start to get in 1951, will come along quite rapidly. It seems to me that 1951 is a somewhat indefinite date. The nearest part of 1951 is only four months away, and if we receive those vessels in the early part of 1951 that will be fairly satisfactory. I wish, however, that the minister would be a little more specific, and instead of saying they will be delivered in 1951 tell us when in 1951 they will be delivered.
When the minister was speaking about the destroyers and other naval vessels which were being put back into commission, the ones which people say have been in mothballs, he said that they would be put into commission fairly rapidly. At that time I asked him if he could tell us when, and he said no. These ships are in existence. It is a matter of reconditioning them, and putting certain new armaments on them. In the past as soon as one ship has been put into commission, it has been immediately announced by the defence department with a great hurrah. I cannot see any reason why the minister cannot tell us when these vessels which are being recommissioned will be back in service. It is not much use to be told that they will be put into service when it might be a year or two years from now. Why can we not be told when they will be back in service? I cannot see any requirement of security or anything else to prevent it.
I have already spoken about the army to some extent, but when the discussion was going on this afternoon in connection with commitments and the fact that under the Atlantic pact we might be required to send forces to any country which was attacked, it struck me that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. . Pearson) had commenced to deal with that question a few days ago. During the debate on the speech from the throne I had asked a question about the attitude of our government in regard to the dispersion of our forces in the event of various other Koreas breaking out in different places.


I think it was absolutely essential that we send ground forces to Korea. I am only sorry that we took so long to say we would do it. But that does not necessarily mean that we should send forces to every place in the world when trouble breaks out. As a matter of fact, I can think of no surer way of keeping ourselves weak than sending 6,000 men to Korea, 1,000 to Formosa, 2,000 to Indo-China, 3,000 to Persia, and so forth. We should have a policy in connection with this matter, and the government should state the policy in regard to sending forces hither and yon where trouble might break out.
As I say, the minister started to answer this in one part of his speech, but was diverted by a question and did not come back to that matter. I should like to hear what he has to say on that particular subject, and whether we have any policy on it.
Turning briefly to the air force, I believe we had almost as bad a picture, so far as it was concerned when the Korean outbreak came, as we had for the army. We had no fighter squadrons we could send, and we had no bomber squadrons. What we did send was a small squadron of transport planes which was supplemented with some planes we rented from the C.P.R. That is all we could do because we had nobody who could fight. Now we find that there is a program of expansion so far as equipment for the air force is concerned. We should be told a little more definitely than we have been when this expansion program is going to start to bear results. I believe the minister said the interceptor squadrons would be increased threefold. When are those increases going to be effective? The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) pointed out this afternoon that the rate of recruiting which the minister said they expected would mean that it would be four and a half years before the air force reached its ceiling. You see that is a different picture from the one presented by the minister when he says that interceptor squadrons will be increased threefold, other squadrons will be increased so many fold, and the rate of production of the Orenda engine will be increased five hundred per cent. Those things may sound all right to a person who is not thinking about the matter, but they do not mean anything. They are not the kind of figures we should get. These percentages and general statements are no good.
So far as the reserve forces ate concerned, I have said enough about them. I should like to say one word about civil defence. As the minister knows, for the past two or three years I have been urging that something definite should be done about this

matter. I was glad to read in the newspaper about a provincial conference which was held dealing with the subject. Upon looking over these estimates which we are asked to pass, I see no mention whatever of any vote for civil defence. A little while ago the minister said that it would likely be a local matter. I hope the dominion government is not going to leave this matter almost entirely to the municipalities and the provinces, with no central direction. If the dominion assumes its proper responsibility in the matter of civil defence, it must have some funds voted to support it. As I say, I do not see anything in these estimates before us, so I should like the minister to explain why. So far as the dominion is concerned, how are civil defence matters going to be financed?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should answer at once the question with regard to financing the federal part of civil defence. It will be provided for out of the administration vote for the department. Perhaps I should add that already representatives of the provinces have arranged a civil defence course on radiation to begin at Borden this month. Successive courses will be held until the spring. We will also be establishing at Borden or at Meaford a civil defence school for representatives of the provinces and municipalities, along the lines of the schools already established in the United Kingdom. This matter is moving along.
With regard to some of the other matters which the hon. gentleman mentioned, he has gone over some of the ground that I have already dealt with in this and other debates, and I do not want to go over it again. He asked about the progressive commissioning of ships. One of the ships, which was in reserve at the time of the Korean incident, has since been commissioned. That is the Nootka. Successively other ships-Crusader, Crescent and Iroquois-will be commissioned as they complete their refits and as crews are recruited and trained or supplied from other sources. That will be a progressive operation relating to the recruitment and training of crews. Later of course there will be the production and installation of the new guns. These will be produced at Sorel.
As to the amount spent on administration and headquarters staff, I should like to call to the attention of the committee that this is the second specific reference to any lack of proper economy on the part of the Department of National Defence with regard to this job.

speechtext:
I should like to follow with some remarks on the subject the other two speakers have dealt with, namely civilian defence. I endorse heartily all that the hon. member for Lanark had to say, from his expert point of view. He outlined to us the dangers of atomic war, the dangers of the use of bacteria and other things. In view of 

the fact that he is so well qualified to speak on those matters, I am going to leave that part to him, merely endorsing every word that he said as something which we should take heed of.
I am, however, interested in what the minister had to say. He pointed out that civilian defence is to be left more or less to the provinces and to the municipalities. We know, from experience in the past, how impossible the situation has been, whether it has been with regard to relief, old age pensions or anything else. It is just a form of passing the buck. I believe that it is a mistake if the dominion government does not take the lead and tell the municipalities and the provincial governments what their part shall be rather than waiting for them to take the lead. I know that the minister possibly did not mean what he said quite in the way he said it, but I am also sure that he is not aware of the urgency of this situation. As the hon. member for Lanark pointed out, it takes time for civilian defence. Time is important. However, this defence appropriation contains no item whatever for civil defence-not one cent, so far as I can see. Therefore the urgency has not yet dawned on the department. The minister has indicated that there is a certain amount of secrecy about it, and certain information he cannot divulge. My only suggestion would be that there should be no secrecy around a matter of such importance to the civil population of Canada as is their own defence. That is one thing you cannot keep secret. The more knowledge imparted to them, and the more they are educated, the better it will be for the people concerned.
The minister knows as well as I do what happened in France during the last war. He knows how the people, lacking leadership, lacking training and lacking civil defence fled in panic from town to town, clogging the roads, hampering the movement of troops, and getting killed into the bargain. The same thing could happen here in Canada; the same panic could take place. I know people say it cannot happen here, that the Russians are too far away; but let me remind the committee that it is only a few years ago a flight of Russians came all the way across northern Canada and landed in the United States, and with planes greatly inferior to the ones they have today. That has been done, and if it has been done once it can be done again. So, do not fool yourselves; do not become complacent and say that it cannot happen here in Canada.
I do feel that civilian defence is as important as military defence. In the next war, wherever it may be, the civilians will be right in the centre of the area of warfare,

right in the target area-and whether it be Canada, the United States or Europe makes no difference. Therefore, bearing that in mind, civilian defence must be carried out in full co-operation with the military defence of the country; and those civil defence measures should be started immediately. The training and supplying of guards and air raid wardens in towns should be commenced, so that they would have some knowledge of communications, learn something about telephones, telegraph, radio and transportation, by road, rail or air, and prepare for the maintenance of supplies of light, power, oil, gas, coal, wood and the like.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Lanark, preparations should be made to find places for the storage of food, and for its distribution later on. The rail strike brought home to us forcefully the fact that some of our towns in Canada are supplied only from week to week. After only a few days one town was calling for more supplies, because it was running short. Another week of the rail strike would have brought that weakness to the fore, and it would have been shown that very few towns in Canada have enough supplies to last them for more than one to three weeks in case of distress conditions, or in the event of war.
A civil defence set-up would be instructed to find out what supplies are available, to list them and to have them in convenient points in case of need. They would also look after water, sanitation, health and the like. I am suggesting this because if a beginning is made in plenty of time I am sure the authorities will receive all the assistance they want from clubs such as the Rotary club, the Gyro club, Kiwanis and others. Their members would be only too willing to help and to be trained; they would be prepared to organize and to submit -to the discipline required for civil defence.
The seriousness of the situation is better known to the minister than it is to us, because the huge appropriation before us is an indication of the urgency and the seriousness of the international situation. The hon. member for Lanark also pointed out that it is possible to minimize the danger from atomic explosion. I believe the cost of informing the public either through the press or the radio or through lectures would be very cheap when compared with the vast results that would accumulate for the protection of our people. I shall not deal more with that aspect of the matter because I think it has been covered fairly well.
My point is that we ought not to rely upon the immunity of Canada from war, and that we should remember at this time we are in
Defence Appropriation Act the danger area. Chaos may be the result if we are not trained to meet the impact of the enemy in our own land.
When reading through the suggestion that has been made for financing the military defence of the country I was somewhat alarmed to find an item of about $28 million for the acquisition of property. I would ask the minister if new properties are to be acquired with this money, if any substantial portion of it is to be used for that purpose, or if the old properties that obviously we had in the last war are to be operative in the next one.
I feel that during the last war Canada had enough properties with which to train the largest army we ever had, and perhaps one larger than we hope to gather together at the present time. Therefore, for the life of me I cannot see why it should be necessary to have an item of $28 million to acquire more properties.
If old properties are to be used, then I suggest to the minister that a real check should be made, particularly on old ranges, to make sure that there is no unexploded ammunition left in the ground. I know it is charged that the accidents at Petawawa and at other camps have been the result of slackness. The same applies to the Vernon camp. It was given up, abandoned, and a wire put around it. Here and there, every mile or so a danger sign was erected, instead of removing the danger from unexploded shells still in the ground. The result was that long after the war was over three young men went on to the area and, while digging, struck one of these unexploded shells, with the result that all three were killed. The department will accept no responsibility. I have taken the matter up with the minister and, while I must say he has done all he can do personally, the legal branch of the department continues to deny all liability. These three boys lost their lives, partially, I say, through the responsibility and neglect of the Department of National Defence and its failure to make sure that these unexploded shells would not go off. I suggest that before these camps are used again they should be covered thoroughly by mine detectors, particularly in the target and storage areas, to make sure that there is no chance of further explosions of this kind.
May I now mention the reserve army, in which I served during the last war. Let me suggest to the minister that if he wants to get more co-operation from the men and officers in the reserve force, greater consideration should be given for the time they give to the reserve army. I know they are allowed

Defence Appropriation Act the time during which they are actually drilling, but sometimes they are in attendance one or two hours before drilling commences, and some must travel ten or twelve miles to reach the drill hall. If some compensation could be given for the time taken in travel to and from the drill hall, and waiting for training to commence, I believe there would be greater co-operation.
Any pay given to the reserves should, in my view, be accepted as an allowable deduction for income tax purposes. The sum is not great, and I understand it cannot be segregated; but if it were considered as an allowable expense it should be so treated. I can assure the minister, as other hon. members have done, that the money that members of the reserve forces receive for the services they render does not by any means cover the expense to which they are put to attend drill, particularly those who are ten miles away.
In conclusion may I suggest that the leader of the opposition rendered excellent service to the people of Canada when he asked that a secret session be held so that we might hear the truth about Korea. Like other hon. members I came here in total ignorance and I am still in ignorance. I have not learned a great deal because we have been kept in the dark. In justice to hon. members who have come long distances and who for five or six months are out of touch with the government, this secret session should be held. We should be told the truth, no matter how unpalatable or unpleasant it is. If we were told the stark, naked truth we would be better able to serve our country. It is up to the government to indicate their confidence in us rather than to treat us like children. I appeal to the minister to consider seriously the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In the course of the discussion of these resolutions it has been obvious that the most attention has been given to the work of the Canadian army. I would point out that at the outset of the session which was called at the beginning of the last war the leader of the opposition pointed out then that Canada was liable to invasion from the north. With the great advances that have been made in the range of aeroplanes such an invasion seems more feasible today; it is hardly likely to be anything more than a diversionary raid which would not require prolonged attention from the army.
However, there is one great danger which I think this country will have to face, particularly if it is involved in a European war. I refer to the danger from submarines. Whatever may be the comparison between our forces and those of other countries, there can [Mr. Jones.l
be no doubt that there are great numbers of submarines in the possession of our potential enemies. The submarine of today is much more powerful than those used during the first and second world wars. It is said that the present-day submarine has a range five times as great as the U-boats of the last war.
I should like to refer to a couple of incidents that took place during the last war around the shores of Newfoundland. One summer's day a submarine or submarines entered Conception bay where there were three or four ships waiting at Bell island to load iron ore for North Sydney. Those ships were sunk at the pier or while waiting at anchorage in the presence of thousands of people. There was a corvette within three miles and Torbay airport was only four or five miles away, yet the submarines escaped.
I am wondering if any provision is being made in these items to provide for improved submarine detection. I happened to be at that spot shortly after those ships were sunk and saw naval vessels trying to locate those submarines. It is a shallow bay and the incident occurred four or five miles inside the headlands, and yet the submarines could not be located there. If they could not be located in such narrow waters, what will happen when they have a greater area in which to hide? I trust that the research department has been making a study of how better to detect submarines.
We shall have to convoy troops and supplies to Europe as was done before. It is well known that a convoy goes only as fast as the slowest ship, and convoys are the principal targets that submarines go after. It is necessary that our submarine detection devices should be powerful and that we should have suitable aircraft and sub-chasers ready to take up the chase. Good work was done by the Canadian navy working out of St. John's and the Royal Canadian Air Force in protecting convoys to Europe.
There are two areas which are particularly dangerous. One is cape Race, the point that most ships make for when coming to America and from which they depart when going to Europe. It is a common sight to see many large ships passing by that cape. That would be one point where packs of submarines would be lying in wait for ships. The strait of Belle Isle is another dangerous point.
In view of the reports that have been published about submarines along the coasts of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and in the Cabot strait, we ought to have a patrol in existence now to watch for submarines. It should be remembered that within a few hours after the last war was declared the

Athenia was sunk in mid-Atlantic. If an enemy were going to make war upon us or upon some European country he would not announce beforehand what he was going to do .but would attack and might have his submarines in the position where they could do the most harm.
There is another matter I should like to speak of and which was referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South in the excellent speech he made this morning. The hon. member referred to our merchant seamen. These men have always felt that they had a grievance. They ran risks equal to if not greater than those faced by the men in the navy or army but they have not been given the same consideration. If they have been injured they receive no pension. I believe that the United States merchant seamen who served during the war were treated the same as the men in the navy.
I ask the minister to give consideration to these men. There is no doubt about the courage of the merchant seamen for some of them were torpedoed two, three or even four times and yet they went back to sea. This is an extremely important service and it deserves every consideration in the way of compensation and other benefits.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on this occasion to tell the committee that on a Sunday afternoon twenty years ago I was taken through a communist school in the city of Toronto where at least 150 children, ranging in age from six to fourteen years, were being instructed by communist instructors how to ridicule their parents, how to worship the Russian state and how to lose any confidence that they might have in the great British empire. In that school were pictures of Stalin draped with red flags. The children of those parents were sitting around playing cards or just talking.
Those children of twenty years ago are now men and women of 26 to 34 years of age. I do not thinik anyone will doubt that many of those young children who were being trained in that school when their minds were so impressionable continued on to Moscow to become more thoroughly trained in propaganda and how to take insidious action against their native land. Those men and women are on the loose in all parts of Canada. Surely the government must be aware of the fact that I am stating. If they are not they should be. I have never had the opportunity of going through the communistic schools in the city of Montreal, but I am positive I am right in saying they are there, and that they are adequately equipped and largely attended year in and year out. These are facts.
Defence Appropriation Act
My constituents and yours, fellow members of the House of Commons, rely on us when we come to parliament to find out what are the facts regarding the possibilities of an attack on the Dominion of Canada by the communist-controlled part of the world. We did not come here for this session simply to listen to a half-baked plan of the Minister of National Defence and salve our conscience that it provides the answers the people are looking for. These are not the questions your constituents ask you, and that applies to members in all parts of the house.
The people of Canada realize that the only reason traitors to this country ended up in Kingston penitentiary for espionage was the fact that the Russians kicked the door off an apartment in the city of Ottawa. That was not because of anything done by the secret service or any part played by the Liberal government. The Russians had to kick a door down. A man had to break away from the Russian embassy, had to plead for protection, and even when he did a very important member of this government at that time gave instructions that the young man should return to his embassy. He did not want to have anything to do with him. The government has taken a great deal of credit for capturing the spies. All they did was to try them and, in my opinion, inadequately sentence them after the Russians had virtually delivered their spies to the gates of our prisons.
What was the sense of going to terrific expenditure to bring members of parliament to this House of Commons for this session? To settle a strike that was already settled? From the expressions on the faces of members of the Liberal party, particularly the cabinet ministers, it was a foregone conclusion that no matter what we said or did the result was going to be exactly as it turned out. The men were going back to work, and they will continue to work. The strike is settled to the satisfaction of the workers involved. That could have been done without bringing members of parliament thousands of miles at terrific expense.
Now we are told that another important subject is the Korean situation. If any member of the house has learned any more about the Korean situation since he arrived here than he knew from the daily newspapers, or why we should vote for more munitions or less munitions, I should like to know what he has learned. Nothing has been divulged here to lead one to believe that we do not have all the armed services necessary to cope with the situation right up to this very minute.
Speaking of communistic trained people in Canada, I wish I could be sent on a mission to Russia to blow up their Niagara falls three

Defence Appropriation Act weeks before an attack with the same kind of training and the same knowledge that they have of this country. I wish the great honour would be given me to blow up a canal similar to the Welland canal. I would certainly blow it. There is not a guard on that life-line of industry at the present time. There is not a guard on the Niagara power plant, the new power plants recently put into operation in the province of Ontario, or anywhere else from coast to coast. There is not a guard on the Welland canal. There is not a guard on the Sault canal. Nevertheless we are brought here in a crisis and we are almost led to believe that there may be some necessity for terrific expenditures. The government is trying to impress upon us that the Russians mean business. We have not got a division of
30,000	men. We have not got a brigade for Korea. No person has told us what a thimbleful we have for the defence of Canada.
I do not suppose we can spare any of our competently trained permanent force men to guard property properly. I do not suppose we can spare the necessary handful from our thimbleful of trained men to guard the Welland canal or the source of power and energy at Niagara. Crisis! How can the people of Canada be convinced that this expenditure is necessary, that this country as a member of the United Nations is playing a part in a serious situation, when things of that nature are not being attended to? The people back home are just ordinary human beings. They are not mind-readers, and today they are perplexed beyond description. They have not the vaguest conception of what is going on. They are being lulled into a false sense of security and safety by the fact that the great parliament of Canada is now in session, and doing nothing but wasting time.

The situation is that no newspaper can convey to the public of Canada where Canada stands at the present time.
I am not simply speaking to hear myself talk or for your benefit either. I am trying to voice the opinions and feelings of Mr. Average Canadian. I feel I am voicing them when I say that I believe Canadians will be rushed into another war without knowing why they are in it, almost precisely as they were in 1914 and in 1939.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They made a good showing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
They made a good showing, and you were not the only man who was there to make a showing. Probably you will not be the last one to go this time either. I believe that Canadians will be rushed into a war with Russia with the concrete evidence we have regarding the attitude of Russia towards the rest of the world, and the reason for fighting the enemy will be the most perplexing that any group of people ever had. Recruiting for the army today, both the permanent force and the Korean brigade, is certainly disgraceful when compared with the thirty thousand men who were recruited, equipped and shipped to Salisbury Plain within thirty days, in 1914. That is due to the fact that while the young people of this country are just as willing to fight in defence of their country today as they were in 1914, they just cannot see why they should enlist; they cannot see the necessity. That has been brought about by the lethargy of this government. The mere fact that the members have been brought back to parliament does not give the young people of Canada any reason why they should volunteer to fight. It is time some person here spoke frankly and was not afraid that Mr. Joe Stalin might learn something he does not know today if we said we were in an awful mess, as we are.
I am only speaking on behalf of the man who is questioning the actions of the cabinet of this country. I hope they will give the press something that will convey to the people of Canada the fact that we are not only being attacked by communists outside Canada. We are also being attacked by a well trained army of communists in Canada, and these are Canadian-born, I am sorry to say.

speechtext:
I wish to raise one point in connection with the general debate, arising from a statement made this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As I understood him-and incidentally it seemed to me the minister was interpreting the section correctly-in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra he said that, under the Atlantic pact, if another nation were attacked the procedure then would be for our parlia-
Defence Appropriation Act ment to be assembled to determine whether there had been an attack, whereupon we would consider in our own discretion what steps we would take. Is that a fair recital of what the minister said? If it is I want to direct this question to him. According to my understanding that is radically different from what was intended and planned under the United Nations Organization. My understanding is that there it was fully intended that there should be definite allotments of forces to be supplied by the various nations, but that this was prevented by the Russian veto. If I am right so far I wish to ask the minister this. Why is it that under the Atlantic pact they are satisfied with an arrangement which seems to me not only infinitely less effective but I would say so ineffective that I cannot think the nations of western Europe will regard it as of much assistance at all? I was in France three weeks ago, and I got some conception of the anxieties they face there. It does seem to me-and I would like the minister's comment on this-that the procedure as he described it this afternoon would involve such delay and such uncertainty that it would be largely nugatory in the sense of any common effort.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I tried to explain this point this afternoon, but I do not mind trying again if there is any doubt in the mind of the hon. member as to what I meant.

speechtext: I thought I understood you.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The situation visualized under the United Nations charter was not the same as that we now have under the North Atlantic pact. Under the United Nations charter article 43 provided for certain specific military forces to be made available for defence against aggression on instructions from the security council. This country, along with other members of the United Nations, accepted that charter, the only condition being that if we were not on the security council, where we would have our say in the determination of aggression, and if our forces were to be used, we would be consulted in the security council before they were used. That was the situation under the United Nations, which was made ineffective by the veto of the U.S.S.R.
Under the North Atlantic pact we have agreed that an attack on one member is an attack on all. Whether that attack has taken place will be decided by the members of the group individually and collectively. That was not our individual decision in this matter; that was the decision taken by all the members of the Atlantic group. An attack on one would be an attack on all, but each member

Defence Appropriation Act reserved the right to determine whether an attack had taken place. If that determination is made by an individual nation, then that individual nation is pledged to take all possible measures to meet that attack, which would be an attack upon itself.
If there is anything more I can say I shall be glad to try to explain further, but I believe I have made the position pretty clear. That is the position which has been accepted by all the members of the pact, including the European countries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would any majority decision be involved? Suppose one nation decided there was no attack and all the others decided there had been an attack. Could that 6ne nation stay out while all the other nations carried on?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The position is that each nation determines whether that obligation it has undertaken by signing this pact is engaged in respect of any particular incident. It remains to each nation to determine whether the obligation into which it has entered has actually been engaged by any particular incident.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did understand the minister this afternoon then, and I am grateful to him for repeating it. The only other thing I should like to say is that when we had this before us months ago, owing to the fact that our imagination was dull, perhaps we did not scrutinize these things as carefully as we might have. I suppose also that that was the most we could get. I do not know whether it is fair to ask the minister this question, so perhaps I had better content myself with expressing my own hope. In the light of the very grave realities, we now see so much more clearly than we did months ago what seems to me to be an obvious weakness in the Atlantic pact as compared with what was at any rate hoped under the United Nations Organization, and my hope is that it might now be strengthened, and I am wondering if there is any such hope.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not admit for one minute that there is any weakness in the obligation we have undertaken in the Atlantic pact in comparison with the obligation we have undertaken under the United Nations charter. The members of the Atlantic pact are a group of nations that have confidence in each other and in their collective will to resist aggression. I think each member of the Atlantic group is also confident that if an attack is made on one member all the others will consider it as unprovoked attack and will,' if the facts are clear-and the facts certainly would be clear if they were those which we have in Korea-take action to meet it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Let me preface this by another question. If the intention of the article in the UN charter had been carried out then would the situation not be, in effect, that any nation that was attacked would know just what it could count on from the other nations, whereas now there is no such knowledge?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think that is the situation, because even under the UN charter if article 43 had been carried out the determination of aggression would be made by the security council, and any one of the five countries on the security council could have vetoed that decision. I think our position under the Atlantic pact is an advance, in fact, on that which we might have had on the security council even if article 43 had been carried into effect, because on that security council we have five permanent members any one of whom had a veto and one of those permanent members was the U.S.S.R.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I gather from what the minister has said, and he has said it before and I think this is a fundamental weakness, that had the U.S.S.R. been at the meeting and exercised her veto we would have been powerless under the UN charter to take steps against the aggression in Korea. Is that a correct interpretation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, the legal situation, as hon. members know, is that if the U.S.S.R. member had been present in the security council when the resolution to determine aggression was before that council, he could have vetoed that resolution. Under the charter of the United Nations, no such resolution would have become effective. There are, however, other ways by which the United Nations could act than through the security council. A special session of the assembly could have been called and recommendations passed which are not obligatory upon the members, but which could be accepted by the members. If the members of the United Nations had desired, that alternative course might have been followed.

I am glad to know there is a backdoor method of preventing aggression in the machinery of the United Nations.
With regard to the Atlantic pact, if a member of the Atlantic community decided in its sovereign powers that an aggression has taken place against any member and decides to place armed forces at the control of the Atlantic community, what machinery is there for commanding those forces? Are they placed under an organization headed by Field Marshal Montgomery, or who is there to take command of those forces?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Very elaborate machinery
has been worked out. There are five regional groups under the North Atlantic treaty, including the western European group which corresponds with the western union. For the purpose of the North Atlantic treaty planning, the western union command under General Montgomery is the corresponding agent for the North Atlantic treaty organization. There are two groups in respect of which Canada is directly involved. They are the North American region and the north Atlantic ocean .region. Our officers sit with those of other countries, and consider plans for our own defence. The five groups all communicate their considerations to the standing group which consists of the chiefs of staff of the United States, the United Kingdom and France or their representatives, under the chairmanship of the United States. They report to the military chiefs of staff of all twelve nations and the chiefs of staff report to the defence ministers.
Ever since the organization of the North Atlantic treaty countries, these groups have been working together in their regions assessing the requirements, assessing available means of defence and discussing plans for defence; and as has been reported to this house on a number of occasions, they have arrived at an over-all plan. On the basis of that plan, which was reported to the council of foreign ministers last May, further developments have since been taking place. There has been a committee of deputies appointed and continuously in session, as was pointed out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. A further meeting of the council of foreign ministers is being held in September, and of defence ministers at Washington in October. There is a very complete, almost too complete, procedure for working out plans and arriving at concrete considerations. Our thought has been that it should be possible to simplify that.
The only place where a commanding officer has been appointed is in the western union which now has, by reference, been made the planning group for the western European region of the North Atlantic treaty. Whether or not further commanding officers will be appointed in advance of an emergency remains to be seen. That can be done very easily by agreement if it is desirable. Even if it is not done in advance, there can be an understanding as to who should be appointed.

to form a chiefs of staff committee, and to set the co-ordinating machinery at work. Presumably those are some of the things that will be discussed on Saturday.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
A chiefs of staff committee
has been set up under the North Atlantic treaty; that is called the military committee. It has met on several occasions and it has an executive group named the standing group, consisting of the chiefs of staff of the United States, France and the United Kingdom or their representatives. They report to the military committee and the military committee reports to the defence ministers.

speechtext:
I was glad to hear the minister, in connection with defence, say he was afraid perhaps the organization at the top was too complete. It may become like our Canadian army with 15,000 training and administrative personnel to only
5,000	fighting troops.
I wanted to go -back to what the minister of external affairs said. It seemed to me the answer he gave to me to support the statement that the Atlantic pact was really better than the UN was because what had been hoped to be accomplished in UN was impossible of accomplishment as a result of the potential veto.
I will now just come back to this point and offer my opinion for what it is worth. It seems to me that if the minister is content to leave the situation as it is now where, as he said, people trust each other and believe they will do the right thing when trouble comes, I like that spirit a great deal. But on the other hand, in the state that things are now in I would feel much happier, and I am sorry that the minister does not take that view, if there were much more in the way of definite understanding as to what is going to happen when trouble comes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is only one other way, Mr. Chairman, in which it could be done under the North Atlantic pact, as I understand it; and that is by having the decision taken by the North Atlantic council in respect of the determination of an aggression, by a majority of the council, by which the minority would be bound. We have not yet reached that point in -any international committee of this kind that I know of. In effect, I -think it will be found that if aggression of the North Korean kind is committed, there will be no hesitation or doubt on the part of any of the members of the North Atlantic pact.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister is talking just about the question of determining aggression. I am talking about what you do when an aggression is determined.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 7, 1950

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SUSPENSION OP STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 7, 1950
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) announced that he wished to move that the house resolve itself into committee of ways and means tomorrow at eight o'clock. We find that this cannot be done without moving the following motion by leave of the house. I therefore move, seconded by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson):
That the provision of standing order 28 respecting the committee of ways and means be suspended for Thursday, September 7, 1950.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 7, 1950
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 7, 1950
speechtext: The understanding is that the adoption of this motion is only for the purpose of permitting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to introduce his budget at eight, o'clock tomorrow night.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SUSPENSION OP STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 7, 1950
speechtext: That is the understanding, Mr. Speaker; and I understand that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will move the adjournment of that debate. Tomorrow we shall continue the debate on this resolution and proceed with the bill, if possible, if the resolution carries.

Motion agreed to.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
